sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: Claiming Australia: Captain Cook, Tupaia & The Myth of Terra Nullius (1768–1770)
sources.title: Source B (Visual Record): Tupaia's Chart of the Pacific Ocean (c. 1769)
sources.caption: Tupaia's Chart of the Pacific (c. 1769): Drawn aboard HMS Endeavour by Polynesian high priest and master navigator Tupaia, mapping over 70 islands across 3,000 miles of Oceania (British Library Add MS 21593 C).
sources.context: Tupaia joined the Endeavour at Tahiti, using centuries-old Polynesian non-instrument navigation (star paths, ocean swells, and bird flight) to guide Cook through uncharted waters. **Hinge Question:** Why did European imperial histories celebrate Cook as a "lone discoverer" while erasing the indispensable guidance of Polynesian navigator Tupaia?
sources.hinge_question: Why did European imperial histories celebrate Cook as a "lone discoverer" while erasing the indispensable guidance of Polynesian navigator Tupaia?
discussion_ideas: Tupaia's chart demonstrates that Pacific peoples possessed profound geographical and navigational mastery over thousands of miles of ocean, shattering the colonial myth that Europeans discovered an empty, unmapped ocean.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: Claiming Australia: Captain Cook, Tupaia & The Myth of Terra Nullius (1768–1770)
sources.title: Source C (Visual Record): Sydney Parkinson, Eyewitness Sketches of Gweagal Warriors and Material Culture at Botany Bay (April 1770)
sources.caption: Sydney Parkinson, Pencil sketches of Gweagal men, tied bark canoes (nawi), gunyahs (bark dwellings), and carved hardwood shields at Botany Bay, April 1770 (British Library Add MS 9345).
sources.context: Sydney Parkinson made the earliest known European drawings of Australian First Nations people during Cook's landing at Botany Bay, recording two Gweagal warriors with spears and shields. **Hinge Question:** How does Parkinson's visual evidence of canoes, homes, and defensive shields directly contradict the British legal claim that Australia was "terra nullius" (nobody's land)?
sources.hinge_question: How does Parkinson's visual evidence of canoes, homes, and defensive shields directly contradict the British legal claim that Australia was "terra nullius" (nobody's land)?
discussion_ideas: Parkinson's sketches provide undeniable visual proof that Gweagal society possessed complex maritime technology, settled shelters, and territorial defense, disproving the legal justification of terra nullius.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: Claiming Australia: Captain Cook, Tupaia & The Myth of Terra Nullius (1768–1770)
sources.title: Source D (Visual Record): Manuscript Journal of Lieutenant James Cook Claiming New South Wales (22 August 1770)
sources.caption: Manuscript page from Captain James Cook's Endeavour journal, recording the ceremony on Possession Island where he claimed the entire eastern coast of Australia for King George III under the name of New South Wales (National Library of Australia MS 1).
sources.context: At Possession Island in the Torres Strait, Cook hoisted the English flag and fired three volleys of musketry, declaring British sovereignty without consulting any First Nations people. **Hinge Question:** Why did Cook feel legally justified in claiming over 2,000 miles of inhabited coastline based solely on hoisting a flag on an offshore islet?
sources.hinge_question: Why did Cook feel legally justified in claiming over 2,000 miles of inhabited coastline based solely on hoisting a flag on an offshore islet?
discussion_ideas: Cook's journal confirms that Britain claimed eastern Australia through ceremonial imperial performance rather than treaty or purchase, ignoring the presence of hundreds of sovereign First Nations.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: Claiming Australia: Captain Cook, Tupaia & The Myth of Terra Nullius (1768–1770)
sources.title: Source E (Visual & Written Record): Sir William Blackstone on the Legal Classification of Overseas Colonies (1765)
sources.caption: Thomas Gainsborough, Portrait of Sir William Blackstone (1774) with extract from Commentaries on the Laws of England (Book II, Chapter 1, 1765), establishing the legal fiction of terra nullius.
sources.context: Blackstone's Commentaries formed the cornerstone of English imperial law. Because Aboriginal Australians did not build European-style fences or cultivate European crops, British authorities classified Australia as "desert and uncultivated" (terra nullius). **Hinge Question:** Why did English legal theory define land ownership strictly through farming and fencing rather than custodial stewardship?
sources.hinge_question: Why did English legal theory define land ownership strictly through farming and fencing rather than custodial stewardship?
discussion_ideas: Blackstone's legal treatise created the ideological framework that allowed the British Crown to treat inhabited Aboriginal lands as legally empty, denying First Nations customary ownership without firing a shot.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The First Fleet & The Convict Penal Colony (1783–1792)
sources.title: Source A (Visual Record): Louis Garneray, British Prison Hulks Moored in Portsmouth Harbour (c. 1780s)
sources.caption: Louis Garneray, Converted British prison hulks in Portsmouth Harbour (c. 1780s): Dismasted warships used to house overflowing convicts after the loss of the American colonies (National Maritime Museum, BHC1929).
sources.context: Following the American Revolution (1775–1783), Britain lost its primary destination for transported convicts, forcing thousands into squalid, disease-ridden prison hulks along the Thames and southern ports. **Hinge Question:** Why did the British government choose an expensive 15,000-mile voyage to Australia rather than constructing permanent prisons in Britain?
sources.hinge_question: Why did the British government choose an expensive 15,000-mile voyage to Australia rather than constructing permanent prisons in Britain?
discussion_ideas: Garneray's painting highlights the intolerable overcrowding and squalor of prison hulks that compelled the British government to establish a distant penal colony to permanently remove convicts.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The First Fleet & The Convict Penal Colony (1783–1792)
sources.title: Source B (Visual Record): Journal of Surgeon Arthur Bowes Smyth aboard the Lady Penrhyn (1787–1788)
sources.caption: Manuscript title page of Arthur Bowes Smyth's First Fleet journal aboard the transport Lady Penrhyn (1787–1789), recording medical treatment, rations, and births during the voyage (National Library of Australia MS 4568).
sources.context: Bowes Smyth served as surgeon to over 100 female convicts aboard the Lady Penrhyn. **Hinge Question:** How does Bowes Smyth's meticulous medical record reflect Governor Phillip's emphasis on convict survival and health during the voyage?
sources.hinge_question: How does Bowes Smyth's meticulous medical record reflect Governor Phillip's emphasis on convict survival and health during the voyage?
discussion_ideas: Bowes Smyth's journal demonstrates that strict sanitation, regular deck exercise, and fresh food stops at Rio and Cape Town enabled the First Fleet to achieve an unprecedented survival rate of over 97%.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The First Fleet & The Convict Penal Colony (1783–1792)
sources.title: Source C (Visual Record): Francis Fowkes, Convict Sketch and Plan of Sydney Cove (16 April 1788)
sources.caption: Francis Fowkes, "Sketch & Description of the Settlement at Sydney Cove Port Jackson" (16 April 1788): Drawn by a convict just three months after landing, showing camps, stores, and clearing parties (State Library of NSW).
sources.context: After finding Botany Bay exposed and waterless, Governor Phillip relocated to Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788. Fowkes, a convict tradesman, surveyed the layout. **Hinge Question:** Why did Governor Phillip prioritize clearing land for military barracks and storehouses rather than building convict shelters?
sources.hinge_question: Why did Governor Phillip prioritize clearing land for military barracks and storehouses rather than building convict shelters?
discussion_ideas: Fowkes' plan shows how the British immediately organized the landscape around military defense and food security, enclosing convict labor around the Tank Stream to prevent escapes.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: Frontier Warfare: Smallpox, Bennelong & Pemulwuy’s Resistance (1788–1802)
sources.title: Source C (Visual Record): Portrait of Woollarawarre Bennelong in European Dress (c. 1798)
sources.caption: Attributed to James Neagle, Portrait of Woollarawarre Bennelong in European dress (c. 1798): Captured on Phillip's orders in 1789, Bennelong became a cultural mediator and traveled to England before returning to Sydney (Mitchell Library, State Library of NSW).
sources.context: Governor Phillip kidnapped Bennelong in 1789 to establish communication. Bennelong mastered English, negotiated between cultures, and visited London in 1792, but struggled upon returning to find acceptance in either society. **Hinge Question:** Did Bennelong's adoption of European clothing and diplomacy represent cultural collaboration or a strategic survival effort for his people?
sources.hinge_question: Did Bennelong's adoption of European clothing and diplomacy represent cultural collaboration or a strategic survival effort for his people?
discussion_ideas: The portrait of Bennelong highlights the complex, difficult position of Indigenous cultural intermediaries, who adopted European manners to negotiate for their people while enduring deep personal and cultural dislocation.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: Frontier Warfare: Smallpox, Bennelong & Pemulwuy’s Resistance (1788–1802)
sources.title: Source D (Visual Record): Contemporary Engraving of Bidjigal Warrior in Bark Canoe (c. 1798)
sources.caption: Engraving of an Indigenous warrior spearfishing in a bark canoe (nawi) on Port Jackson, published in David Collins, An Account of the English Colony in New South Wales (1798).
sources.context: While Bennelong sought diplomatic mediation, Bidjigal warrior Pemulwuy led a ferocious 12-year guerrilla war against British settlement across the Hawkesbury and Parramatta basins from 1790 to 1802. **Hinge Question:** Why did Pemulwuy's followers believe he had supernatural spiritual immunity against British musket fire, and how did that belief sustain his guerrilla war?
sources.hinge_question: Why did Pemulwuy's followers believe he had supernatural spiritual immunity against British musket fire, and how did that belief sustain his guerrilla war?
discussion_ideas: Collins' engraving demonstrates the extraordinary physical skill and mobility of warriors like Pemulwuy, who utilized the waterways and rugged bush terrain to wage a devastating campaign of resistance against British outposts.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The Frontier Wars, Pastoral Expansion & The Black War (1803–1840)
sources.title: Source B (Visual Record): Governor George Arthur's Pictorial Proclamation Board (c. 1829)
sources.caption: Governor George Arthur's Proclamation Board (c. 1829): Pictorial broadsheet issued during the Black War in Van Diemen's Land, designed to communicate through pictures that British law offered equal justice and punishment to both races (Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery).
sources.context: Governor Arthur ordered painted boards nailed to trees during the Black War to show that white settlers and Indigenous people would be treated equally under British law. **Hinge Question:** Why did Governor Arthur depict "equal justice" on pictorial boards at the very moment he was declaring martial law and mobilizing 2,200 armed men in the Black Line to drive Indigenous Tasmanians from their lands?
sources.hinge_question: Why did Governor Arthur depict "equal justice" on pictorial boards at the very moment he was declaring martial law and mobilizing 2,200 armed men in the Black Line to drive Indigenous Tasmanians from their lands?
discussion_ideas: Arthur's proclamation board presents an idealized fiction of equal legal protection that completely contradicted the brutal reality of martial law, settler vigilantism, and the military Black Line.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The Frontier Wars, Pastoral Expansion & The Black War (1803–1840)
sources.title: Source E (Visual Record): Deposition of William Hobbs on the Myall Creek Massacre (9 July 1838)
sources.caption: Handwritten letter from station superintendent William Hobbs to Police Magistrate Edward Denny Day (9 July 1838), reporting the unprovoked murder of 28 unarmed Wirrayaraay women, children, and elders at Myall Creek Station (State Archives of NSW).
sources.context: On 10 June 1838, a gang of 11 white stockmen bound and murdered 28 defenseless Wirrayaraay people. Hobbs bravely reported the crime, leading to an unprecedented trial where seven perpetrators were convicted and hanged. **Hinge Question:** Why was the conviction of the Myall Creek perpetrators a unique anomaly in 19th-century colonial Australian history?
sources.hinge_question: Why was the conviction of the Myall Creek perpetrators a unique anomaly in 19th-century colonial Australian history?
discussion_ideas: Hobbs' deposition provides indispensable legal evidence of the Myall Creek Massacre, which stood as an extraordinary exception where colonial courts held white stockmen accountable for mass murder.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The Gold Rush, Eureka Stockade & The Legacy of Colonisation (1851–1901)
sources.title: Source B (Visual Record): Colony of Victoria Gold Mining Licence Issued to Raffaello Carboni (17 October 1854)
sources.caption: Official Colony of Victoria Gold License No. 134 issued to Eureka Stockade leader Raffaello Carboni on 17 October 1854 for £2 (three months), signed by Commissioner G. A. Amos and printed by John Ferres at the Government Printing Office (Public Record Office Victoria).
sources.context: Miners were compelled to pay exorbitant fees and carry this physical paper licence at all times, subject to twice-weekly armed police 'digger hunts'. This exact licence was issued to Italian-born digger leader Raffaello Carboni just weeks before the Eureka uprising. **Hinge Question:** Why was the requirement to produce a physical licence on demand so deeply resented by free miners?
sources.hinge_question: Why was the requirement to produce a physical licence on demand so deeply resented by free miners?
discussion_ideas: This authentic 1854 licence proves how the colonial government extracted direct taxation from diggers while denying them political representation, making armed rebellion at Eureka inevitable.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The Gold Rush, Eureka Stockade & The Legacy of Colonisation (1851–1901)
sources.title: Source C (Visual Record): Charles Doudiet, Swearing Allegiance to the Southern Cross at Eureka (1854)
sources.caption: Charles Doudiet, "Swearing allegiance to the Southern Cross" (1 December 1854): Peter Lalor stands on a stump with drawn sword beneath the Eureka flag as 500 miners raise their weapons in rebellion (Art Gallery of Ballarat).
sources.context: On 1 December 1854, over 500 miners knelt beneath the blue-and-white Southern Cross flag and swore: "We swear by the Southern Cross to stand truly by each other, and fight to defend our rights and liberties." Two days later, British troops stormed the stockade, killing 22 diggers. **Hinge Question:** Why did the Eureka rebellion become the foundational myth of Australian democracy despite being a military defeat?
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Eureka rebellion become the foundational myth of Australian democracy despite being a military defeat?
discussion_ideas: Doudiet's watercolor captures the defining moment of democratic solidarity at Eureka, demonstrating that armed resistance against colonial oppression accelerated the introduction of universal male suffrage and the secret ballot.

sources.unitTitle: The History of Australia: First Nations, Colonisation & Resistance (1770–1901)
sources.lessonTitle: The Gold Rush, Eureka Stockade & The Legacy of Colonisation (1851–1901)
sources.title: Source E (Visual Record): Aborigines Progressive Association, Day of Mourning & Protest Manifesto (26 January 1938)
sources.caption: Official printed resolution flyer for the 150th Anniversary Day of Mourning & Protest, held at the Australian Hall in Sydney on 26 January 1938 by the Aborigines Progressive Association (Mitchell Library, State Library of NSW).
sources.context: On Australia's 150th anniversary, while official reenactments celebrated Governor Phillip's landing, First Nations leaders Jack Patten and William Ferguson held a counter-conference declaring 26 January a national Day of Mourning. **Hinge Question:** Why did Indigenous leaders choose the 150th anniversary of the First Fleet to launch their political campaign for constitutional equality?
sources.hinge_question: Why did Indigenous leaders choose the 150th anniversary of the First Fleet to launch their political campaign for constitutional equality?
discussion_ideas: The 1938 Day of Mourning resolution marked a turning point in First Nations political resistance, confronting the celebratory myth of British settlement with the reality of 150 years of dispossession and demanding equal human rights.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?
sources.title: Source A: The McMahon-Hussein Correspondence Territorial Boundaries Map (1915–1916)
sources.caption: Cartographic map delineating the proposed borders of an independent Arab state pledged by Sir Henry McMahon to Sharif Hussein of Mecca (1915–1916).
sources.context: British High Commissioner McMahon promised British recognition of Arab independence in exchange for an Arab armed revolt against Ottoman forces.
sources.provenance: The National Archives, Kew (FO 371/2486), British Arab Bureau records, 1916.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the omission of explicit reference to Palestine in McMahon's letters trigger decades of bitter diplomatic dispute?
discussion_ideas: Source A strongly supports the accusation of bad faith by showing how vague geographical exclusions allowed Britain to promise overlapping territorial sovereignty to both Sharif Hussein and European imperial allies simultaneously.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?
sources.title: Source B: The Sykes-Picot Agreement Partition Map (May 1916)
sources.caption: Signed by Sir Mark Sykes and François Georges-Picot, partitioning Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire into direct and indirect zones of British and French imperial influence.
sources.context: Secret diplomatic convention negotiated between Britain and France with Russian consent during the First World War.
sources.provenance: The National Archives, Kew (FO 93/110/68), 16 May 1916.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the secret Sykes-Picot Agreement provoke enduring Arab resentment when its terms were exposed by the Bolsheviks in 1917?
discussion_ideas: Source B is exceptionally valuable because it provides direct documentary proof that British imperial strategists prioritized territorial division with France over their contemporaneous pledges of self-determination made to Arab leaders fighting the Ottomans.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?
sources.title: Source C: The Balfour Declaration Official Letter (November 1917)
sources.caption: Official letter from Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour to Lord Walter Rothschild conveying the British War Cabinet's sympathy with Jewish Zionist aspirations.
sources.context: Official public statement issued by the British government during the First World War.
sources.provenance: British Library, London (Add MS 41178), 2 November 1917.
sources.hinge_question: How did the phrasing 'national home for the Jewish people' deliberately create ambiguity regarding future statehood?
discussion_ideas: The British government sought to rally worldwide Jewish sympathy—particularly in the United States and revolutionary Russia—behind the Allied war effort, while securing a vital strategic buffer adjacent to the Suez Canal under British imperial protection.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?
sources.title: Source D: Archival Panorama of British Mandate Jerusalem (c. 1918–1920)
sources.caption: Panoramic landscape photograph of British Mandate Jerusalem looking toward the Old City and the Dome of the Rock from the Mount of Olives (c. 1920).
sources.context: Photographic record of Jerusalem under the British Mandate.
sources.provenance: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (Bain Collection LC-DIG-matpc-05743), c. 1920.
sources.hinge_question: How did Jerusalem's shared sacred geography make peaceful partition virtually impossible under British colonial administration?
discussion_ideas: While Source D accurately depicts the monumental religious landscape of Jerusalem that made compromise impossible, as an official topographical record it masks the volatile intercommunal civil violence and economic boycotts brewing on the ground.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?
sources.title: Source E: Theodor Herzl, Founder of the Modern Zionist Movement
sources.caption: Austro-Hungarian journalist Theodor Herzl, author of 'Der Judenstaat' (1896) and convenor of the First Zionist Congress in Basel, 1897.
sources.context: Portrait of Theodor Herzl, who formulated political Zionism in response to European anti-Semitism.
sources.provenance: Central Zionist Archives, Jerusalem (PHG/1012), c. 1897.
sources.hinge_question: How did Herzl's experience of anti-Semitism in Europe convince him that assimilation could never guarantee Jewish safety?
discussion_ideas: Source E illustrates that political Zionism was framed as an urgent, modern national liberation movement driven by the realization that European anti-Semitism was structural and incurable through civic assimilation alone.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?
sources.title: Source A: The Sykes-Picot Agreement Partition Map (8 May 1916)
sources.caption: Primary map of the secret Sykes-Picot Agreement signed on 8 May 1916 by Sir Mark Sykes and François Georges-Picot, dividing the Middle East into British and French spheres of influence.
sources.hinge_question: Study Source A. Using the partition map, explain why the secret Anglo-French division of the Middle East in the Sykes-Picot Agreement laid the groundwork for decades of border conflicts and Arab betrayal.
discussion_ideas: Source A shows how Britain and France carved up the Ottoman Empire using arbitrary straight lines that ignored historic ethnic, tribal, and religious communities. By placing regions like Palestine under international administration and creating artificial borders, the agreement directly contradicted British wartime pledges of independence made to the Arabs in the McMahon-Hussein Correspondence, creating deep-rooted resentment and instability across the region.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.1: The End of the British Mandate and the Creation of Israel, 1945–1949
sources.title: Source A: The SS Exodus 1947 Arriving in Haifa Harbour
sources.caption: The battered immigrant ship SS Exodus 1947, carrying over 4,500 Holocaust survivors, escorted by the Royal Navy into Haifa before passengers were forcibly returned to Germany.
sources.context: The Haganah ship Exodus sailed from France with 4,514 Jewish refugees without immigration certificates.
sources.provenance: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, courtesy of National Archives and Records Administration (USHMM 24195), July 1947.
sources.hinge_question: How did the British naval blockade of immigrant ships like the Exodus become an international public relations disaster for Clement Attlee's government?
discussion_ideas: Source A demonstrates that the Haganah intentionally deployed unarmed refugee ships packed with European Holocaust survivors to expose the cruelty of British immigration quotas before visiting United Nations investigators.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.1: The End of the British Mandate and the Creation of Israel, 1945–1949
sources.title: Source B: David Ben-Gurion Declaring Israeli Independence (14 May 1948)
sources.caption: David Ben-Gurion reading the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel beneath a portrait of Theodor Herzl at the Tel Aviv Museum on 14 May 1948.
sources.context: David Ben-Gurion read the Israeli Declaration of Independence on 14 May 1948.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office (GPO D1-073), 14 May 1948.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the declaration of statehood made hours before the British Mandate officially expired at midnight on 14 May 1948?
discussion_ideas: Ben-Gurion deliberately staged the ceremony beneath Theodor Herzl's image to visually establish historical continuity, affirming that the new state was the legitimate culmination of fifty years of political Zionist struggle and divine national redemption.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.1: The End of the British Mandate and the Creation of Israel, 1945–1949
sources.title: Source C: The King David Hotel Bombing Ruins (22 July 1946)
sources.caption: The collapsed southwestern wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem following the Irgun bomb attack on 22 July 1946, killing 91 British, Arab, and Jewish civil servants and soldiers.
sources.context: The Irgun detonated 350kg of explosives in the basement of the King David Hotel on 22 July 1946, killing 91 people.
sources.provenance: Imperial War Museum, London / British Mandate Police Archives, 22 July 1946.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Irgun target the King David Hotel specifically rather than a British military garrison?
discussion_ideas: Source C is exceptionally useful because the physical devastation of the British administrative and military headquarters provides direct visual proof of the Irgun's capability to strike the nerve-centre of imperial control, destroying Britain's illusion of maintaining public order.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.1: The End of the British Mandate and the Creation of Israel, 1945–1949
sources.title: Source D: The Sergeants Affair Aftermath in Netanya (July 1947)
sources.caption: British soldiers examining the booby-trapped eucalyptus grove near Netanya where the Irgun hanged British sergeants Mervyn Paice and Clifford Martin in retaliation for executions of Jewish militants.
sources.context: In July 1947, the Irgun executed two abducted British intelligence sergeants in retaliation for British executions.
sources.provenance: Imperial War Museum, London (IWM NYP 68066), 31 July 1947.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the hanging of the British sergeants destroy public and political support in Britain for maintaining the Palestine Mandate?
discussion_ideas: Source D is profoundly useful because it captures the brutal insurgency tactics that eroded the British domestic public's willingness to sustain financial debt and military casualties to maintain order between warring communities in Palestine.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.1: The End of the British Mandate and the Creation of Israel, 1945–1949
sources.title: Source E: United Nations Partition Plan for Palestine (Resolution 181)
sources.caption: Official cartographic projection of the UN General Assembly Resolution 181 partition proposal: 56% allocated for a Jewish state, 43% for an Arab state, and an international regime (Corpus Separatum) for Jerusalem.
sources.context: On 29 November 1947, the UN General Assembly voted to partition Palestine into separate Arab and Jewish states.
sources.provenance: United Nations Archives, New York (Map No. 93(b)), November 1947.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Arab Higher Committee reject UN Resolution 181 as fundamentally unjust to the indigenous majority?
discussion_ideas: Source E illustrates that both proposed states were fractured into non-contiguous enclaves with indefensible borders and interwoven populations, ensuring that any attempt to establish sovereignty would instantly trigger violent clashes over vital roads and towns.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.2: The Creation of Israel, the 1948–49 War & The Palestinian Refugee Crisis
sources.title: Source A: UN Ad Hoc Committee Draft Partition Proposals (1947)
sources.caption: Cartographic comparison of the UNSCOP Majority Plan (partition with economic union) versus the Minority Plan (federal single state with autonomous cantons).
sources.context: In 1947, the UN considered two solutions: full partition versus a single federal state.
sources.provenance: United Nations Ad Hoc Committee on the Palestinian Question (A/AC.14/32), October 1947.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the UN reject the federal single-state model in favor of full partition in November 1947?
discussion_ideas: Source A is extremely reliable as an official United Nations legal record showing the actual legislative alternatives debated by member states; it demonstrates that partition was chosen not because it was ideal, but because shared binational governance was judged completely unattainable.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.2: The Creation of Israel, the 1948–49 War & The Palestinian Refugee Crisis
sources.title: Source B: Displaced Palestinian Families in Khan Yunis Camp (1948–1949)
sources.caption: UNRWA archival photograph of a displaced Palestinian mother and young child standing outside makeshift tent shelters in the Khan Yunis refugee camp in Gaza (1948–1949).
sources.context: Over 200,000 Palestinian refugees flooded into the narrow Gaza Strip following the 1948 war.
sources.provenance: UNRWA Photographic Archive (Gaza-1948-KY), 1948–1949.
sources.hinge_question: How did the permanence of refugee tent camps undermine Arab hopes of an immediate return to their villages?
discussion_ideas: Source B is profoundly useful because it captures the squalid, dehumanizing conditions endured by hundreds of thousands of displaced non-combatants, illustrating how the war permanently transformed thriving agrarian communities into destitute refugees dependent on international charity.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.2: The Creation of Israel, the 1948–49 War & The Palestinian Refugee Crisis
sources.title: Source C: The 1949 Armistice Green Line Boundaries Map
sources.caption: Map depicting the 1949 Armistice Agreements (Green Line) following the war: Israel expanded to 78% of Mandate territory; Jordan annexed the West Bank; Egypt administered the Gaza Strip.
sources.context: Bilateral armistice agreements were signed in Rhodes in 1949, establishing the Green Line.
sources.provenance: United Nations Truce Supervision Organization (UNTSO), Rhodes, 1949.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the 1949 armistice agreements fail to create permanent, recognized international borders?
discussion_ideas: Source C is highly reliable because it records the precise military armistice lines negotiated under UN supervision; however, it reflects a temporary cessation of hostilities rather than a de jure peace treaty recognized by neighboring Arab states.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.2: The Creation of Israel, the 1948–49 War & The Palestinian Refugee Crisis
sources.title: Source D: Jewish Immigrants Arriving in Haifa Port (February 1949)
sources.caption: Thousands of Jewish immigrants arriving at Haifa Port aboard the Pan Yorkshire (February 1949) greeted by crowds beneath a Hebrew banner reading "ברוכים הבאים" (Welcome).
sources.context: Between May 1948 and 1951, Israel doubled its Jewish population by absorbing nearly 700,000 immigrants.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office (GPO 997008136796005171), February 1949.
sources.hinge_question: How did the rapid influx of nearly 700,000 Jewish immigrants explain Israel's refusal to permit Palestinian refugees to return?
discussion_ideas: Source D demonstrates that as hundreds of thousands of Jewish refugees were resettled into vacant homes and lands across Israel, the physical reality on the ground was irrevocably altered, rendering the physical return of Palestinian refugees in Source D politically and demographically impossible for Israel.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.2: The Creation of Israel, the 1948–49 War & The Palestinian Refugee Crisis
sources.title: Source E: UNRWA Emergency Bread & Ration Distribution to Displaced Palestinian Refugees (c. 1949)
sources.caption: Archival photograph from the UNRWA Film & Photo Archive showing Palestinian refugee women and children in a temporary tent camp queuing to receive emergency flour and daily bread rations under UN General Assembly Resolution 302.
sources.context: UNRWA was established by UN Resolution 302 to provide relief for Palestinian refugees.
sources.provenance: Official documentary photograph by the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA), c. 1949–1950. UN Archives.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Arab states insist on creating a dedicated agency (UNRWA) rather than folding Palestinian refugees into the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)?
discussion_ideas: Source E reveals that displaced Palestinian refugees lived in severe destitution in tent encampments, completely dependent on emergency international aid and daily UNRWA bread distributions for their basic survival.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.2: The Creation of Israel, the 1948–49 War & The Palestinian Refugee Crisis
sources.title: Source A: Israeli Troops in Heavy Fighting During the 1948 War
sources.caption: Primary Photograph: Israeli soldiers in combat during the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.
sources.hinge_question: Study Source A. What does this photograph reveal about the fighting conditions facing the newly formed IDF, and how was Israel able to defeat the five invading Arab armies in 1948–49?
discussion_ideas: Source A reflects the mobilization and discipline of the newly formed IDF. Despite initial disadvantages in heavy weaponry, Israel benefited from unified political command under Ben-Gurion, superior wartime motivation defending their immediate survival, and the decisive four-week UN truce in June 1948, which allowed Israel to import modern rifles, machine guns, and fighter aircraft from Czechoslovakia, turning the tactical tide against divided Arab forces.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.3: Increased Tension, Nasser, and the Suez Crisis, 1955–1963
sources.title: Source A: Political Cartoon on Nasser Controlling the Canal (1956)
sources.caption: Fritz Behrendt political cartoon 'Der Mann am Hahnen' ('The Man at the Tap', 1956), depicting President Gamal Abdel Nasser turning off the Suez Canal oil valve to Western Europe.
sources.context: British Prime Minister Anthony Eden viewed Nasser's nationalization of the Suez Canal as a direct threat to British power.
sources.provenance: Punch Magazine / British Cartoon Archive, University of Kent (IL0156), August 1956.
sources.hinge_question: How did Western political cartoons frame Egyptian canal nationalization as economic blackmail threatening European industry?
discussion_ideas: The cartoonist sought to mobilize Western public hostility against Nasser by framing canal nationalization not as legitimate anti-colonial sovereignty, but as dangerous economic extortion threatening the lifeblood and industrial fuel supplies of Western Europe.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.3: Increased Tension, Nasser, and the Suez Crisis, 1955–1963
sources.title: Source B: British Psychological Warfare Propaganda Leaflet (November 1956)
sources.caption: British psychological warfare propaganda leaflet dropped over Egyptian cities during Operation Musketeer, depicting Nasser hiding behind a young civilian soldier (November 1956).
sources.context: President Nasser delivered his historic three-hour address in Alexandria announcing canal nationalization.
sources.provenance: The National Archives, Kew (FO 953/1689), British Psychological Warfare Branch, 1956.
sources.hinge_question: How did British aerial leaflets use psychological warfare to undermine Egyptian civilian support for Nasser during the Anglo-French assault?
discussion_ideas: Source B reveals how Britain utilized aerial propaganda drops to bypass Egyptian state censorship, attempting to fracture public unity and convince civilians that Nasser's reckless nationalization had brought unnecessary military devastation upon Egypt.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.3: Increased Tension, Nasser, and the Suez Crisis, 1955–1963
sources.title: Source C: Front Page of Al-Ahram Announcing Nationalization (27 July 1956)
sources.caption: Front page of Egyptian daily newspaper Al-Ahram declaring in banner headlines: 'We Have Nationalized the Suez Canal Company' following Nasser's speech in Alexandria.
sources.context: On 26 July 1956, Nasser announced the nationalization of the Suez Canal Company to fund the Aswan High Dam.
sources.provenance: Al-Ahram Archives, Cairo, Issue No. 25482, 27 July 1956.
sources.hinge_question: Why was nationalizing the canal viewed by Egyptians as an essential act of national sovereignty rather than mere economic policy?
discussion_ideas: Source C is immensely useful because its triumphalist tone and celebratory headlines capture the immense nationalist pride felt by Egyptians, who viewed taking control of the canal as reclaiming their sovereign wealth from decades of imperial exploitation.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.3: Increased Tension, Nasser, and the Suez Crisis, 1955–1963
sources.title: Source D: British RAF Reconnaissance Photograph over Port Said (5 November 1956)
sources.caption: British Royal Air Force aerial photograph capturing dense black smoke rising from burning oil storage tanks beside the Suez Canal entrance at Port Said following Anglo-French air strikes (IWM MH 23509).
sources.context: Aerial reconnaissance photograph taken by the RAF showing oil storage facilities burning at the entrance to the Suez Canal at Port Said in November 1956.
sources.provenance: Royal Air Force aerial photographic reconnaissance unit, Port Said, 5 November 1956 (Imperial War Museum MH 23509).
sources.hinge_question: How does the synchronized coordination between Israeli and British forces on this map expose the secret Sèvres collusion?
discussion_ideas: Source D is very useful because its clear aerial view provides authentic evidence of the heavy physical destruction inflicted on Egypt's port infrastructure, directly demonstrating the intensity of the allied bombing campaign along the canal.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 1.3: Increased Tension, Nasser, and the Suez Crisis, 1955–1963
sources.title: Source E: British Centurion Tanks in Port Said Streets (November 1956)
sources.caption: British Centurion tanks of the 6th Royal Tank Regiment advancing through the war-damaged commercial streets of Port Said during Operation Musketeer.
sources.context: British forces landed in Port Said under Operation Musketeer before being forced into an abrupt withdrawal by US pressure.
sources.provenance: Imperial War Museum, London (IWM FLM 3478), November 1956.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the military success of the Anglo-French assault turn into a catastrophic political defeat?
discussion_ideas: Source E is highly reliable as an official photographic record of British mechanized firepower deployed in Egyptian urban centers; however, it obscures the reality that Britain was diplomatically isolated and economically powerless once Washington refused to back the pound.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.1 Enquiry: How Did Water, Border Raids, and Rhetoric Make a Second Arab-Israeli War Inevitable? (1964–1967)
sources.title: Source A: President Nasser During the Non-Aligned Summit (1962)
sources.caption: President Gamal Abdel Nasser photographed in Belgrade articulating his doctrine of Arab socialism, anti-imperialism, and leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement.
sources.context: President Nasser projected Egypt as the leading force of pan-Arab nationalism and the Non-Aligned Movement.
sources.provenance: Museum of Yugoslav History / Stevan Kragujević Collection, Belgrade, 1962.
sources.hinge_question: How did Nasser's prestige as a global anti-imperialist leader trap him into escalatory rhetoric against Israel in May 1967?
discussion_ideas: Projecting sovereign stature enabled Nasser to extract massive Soviet economic and military hardware while positioning Egypt as an untouchable superpower within Arab politics, which later made any public retreat before Israel unthinkable.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.1 Enquiry: How Did Water, Border Raids, and Rhetoric Make a Second Arab-Israeli War Inevitable? (1964–1967)
sources.title: Source B: Causal Diagram of Syrian-Sponsored Fatah Infiltration & Israeli Reprisals (1965–1967)
sources.caption: Flowchart diagram illustrating the cycle of Syrian-backed Fatah guerrilla raids across the armistice border and the escalating Israeli military retaliation culminating in the Samu raid.
sources.context: Flowchart tracing the chain of causal escalation from Syrian-backed Fatah raids to Israeli reprisals on Samu.
sources.provenance: Department of History Curriculum Analysis, Edexcel Paper 2 Reference Architecture.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Arab states perceive Israel's water diversion to the Negev as an existential economic and military threat?
discussion_ideas: Source B demonstrates that Syrian-backed guerrilla attacks created a destructive cycle of Israeli military counter-attacks, which ultimately targeted Jordanian territory at Samu and shattered trust between neighboring Arab states and Israel.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.1 Enquiry: How Did Water, Border Raids, and Rhetoric Make a Second Arab-Israeli War Inevitable? (1964–1967)
sources.title: Source C: Relief Map of the Golan Heights Artillery Positions (1967)
sources.caption: Topographical relief map illustrating Syrian artillery emplacements perched 1,000 feet above Israeli farming kibbutzim (Ein Gev, Tel Katzir) in the vulnerable Hula Valley below.
sources.context: Syrian forces fortified the Golan Heights, routinely shelling Israeli settlements in the valley below.
sources.provenance: IDF Northern Command Intelligence Division, Nazareth, 1967.
sources.hinge_question: How did the Syrian military use their topographical dominance on the Golan to harass Israeli agricultural communities below?
discussion_ideas: Source C demonstrates that Syrian forces held commanding high ground that left Israeli border kibbutzim in the valley completely exposed to direct artillery observation and bombardment, making normal civilian life virtually impossible without seizing the plateau.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.1 Enquiry: How Did Water, Border Raids, and Rhetoric Make a Second Arab-Israeli War Inevitable? (1964–1967)
sources.title: Source D: Archival Photograph of the Disputed Banyas Spring Headwaters (1967)
sources.caption: Archival view of the Banyas freshwater springs in the Golan foothills, one of three major Jordan River tributaries targeted by Syria's headwaters diversion project.
sources.context: Archival photograph of the Banyas springs in the Golan foothills, which Syria attempted to divert away from Israel's water supply between 1964 and 1966.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office (GPO) Photographic Archive, 1967.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Israel treat the Arab headwaters diversion project as a legitimate casus belli (act of war)?
discussion_ideas: Source D shows the natural freshwater springs that directly fed the National Water Carrier shown in Source B, explaining why Israeli leaders considered Syria's diversion scheme an intolerable threat to their country's vital water supply and used air strikes to destroy it.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.1 Enquiry: How Did Water, Border Raids, and Rhetoric Make a Second Arab-Israeli War Inevitable? (1964–1967)
sources.title: Source E: President Nasser Addressing Egyptian Troops at Bir Gifgafa (22 May 1967)
sources.caption: President Gamal Abdel Nasser addressing Egyptian armed forces and fighter pilots at Bir Gifgafa forward air base in Sinai on 22 May 1967, announcing the blockade of the Straits of Tiran.
sources.context: The United Arab Republic merged Egypt and Syria, but collapsed in 1961 amidst factional disputes.
sources.provenance: Egyptian Ministry of Information / Al-Musawwar Magazine Archives, Cairo, February 1958.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Nasser's public speeches to troops in the Sinai leave Israeli military planners convinced that an Arab invasion was imminent?
discussion_ideas: Source E accurately reflects the militant rhetoric Nasser deployed to rally Arab public opinion; however, privately Egyptian commanders knew their armed forces were bogged down in Yemen and unprepared for full-scale war with Israel.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.2 Enquiry: Why Was the Six-Day War Decided in Three Hours, and Did Nasser Intend to Fight? (May–June 1967)
sources.title: Source A: Israeli Command Entering Jerusalem Through Lions' Gate (7 June 1967)
sources.caption: David Rubinger's iconic photograph showing Defense Minister Moshe Dayan, Chief of Staff Yitzhak Rabin, and General Uzi Narkiss walking through Lions' Gate into the Old City of Jerusalem, 7 June 1967.
sources.context: Defense Minister Moshe Dayan, Chief of Staff Yitzhak Rabin, and Uzi Narkiss entered the Old City through Lions' Gate.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office / David Rubinger (GPO D835-081), 7 June 1967.
sources.hinge_question: How did Moshe Dayan's famous declaration at the Wall ('We have returned to our holiest site, never to part from it again') bind future Israeli governments?
discussion_ideas: Source A is extremely reliable as an official document of the triumphant moment of entry; however, it was carefully composed to project Dayan as the indispensable military hero of the nation, overshadowing the meticulous planning of Prime Minister Eshkol and Chief of Staff Rabin.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.2 Enquiry: Why Was the Six-Day War Decided in Three Hours, and Did Nasser Intend to Fight? (May–June 1967)
sources.title: Source B: Cartographic Map of the Straits of Tiran & Sharm el-Sheikh Blockade (May 1967)
sources.caption: Strategic map highlighting the maritime choke point at the Straits of Tiran and Sharm el-Sheikh, where Egyptian forces blocked Israeli shipping to the port of Eilat on 22 May 1967.
sources.context: President Nasser announced the closure of the Straits of Tiran on 22 May 1967, cutting off Israel's oil route.
sources.provenance: Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs briefing chart, May 1967.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Israel define the closure of the Straits of Tiran as an unambiguous act of war (casus belli)?
discussion_ideas: Source B is profoundly useful because it visually demonstrates Israel's absolute geographic vulnerability at the southern entrance to the Gulf of Aqaba, proving that the closure of the straits severed Israel's primary commercial lifeline to Asia and the Persian Gulf.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.2 Enquiry: Why Was the Six-Day War Decided in Three Hours, and Did Nasser Intend to Fight? (May–June 1967)
sources.title: Source C: Chief Rabbi Goren Blowing the Shofar at the Wall (7 June 1967)
sources.caption: IDF Chief Rabbi Shlomo Goren blowing the shofar while holding a Torah scroll surrounded by paratroopers at the liberated Western Wall on 7 June 1967.
sources.context: Rabbi Shlomo Goren blew the shofar and recited blessings upon reaching the Western Wall.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office (GPO D1-1967), 7 June 1967.
sources.hinge_question: How did Rabbi Goren's messianic interpretation of the conquest give birth to the modern religious Zionist settlement movement?
discussion_ideas: Rabbi Goren sought to sacralize the military triumph by interpreting the capture of Jerusalem not merely as a defensive victory over Arab armies, but as the fulfillment of biblical prophecy and divine redemption for the Jewish people.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.2 Enquiry: Why Was the Six-Day War Decided in Three Hours, and Did Nasser Intend to Fight? (May–June 1967)
sources.title: Source D: Tactical Map of the Egyptian Sinai Collapse (7–8 June 1967)
sources.caption: Tactical military map showing the armored maneuvers of Tal, Yoffe, and Sharon through northern and central Sinai and the trapping of retreating Egyptian divisions at the Mitla and Giddi Passes, 7–8 June 1967.
sources.context: Field Marshal Amer ordered an immediate general retreat, resulting in the encirclement of Egyptian forces.
sources.provenance: Egyptian Ministry of War / Combat Studies Institute Records, Fort Leavenworth, 1967.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Field Marshal Amer's panicked order for general retreat turn an orderly defense into a catastrophic military rout?
discussion_ideas: Source D demonstrates that because the pre-emptive air strike had wiped out Egyptian air defenses on the first morning, retreating Egyptian armored columns shown trapped in the Mitla and Giddi passes had zero protection from relentless Israeli close-air support, turning retreat into an outright massacre.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.2 Enquiry: Why Was the Six-Day War Decided in Three Hours, and Did Nasser Intend to Fight? (May–June 1967)
sources.title: Source E: Israeli Paratroopers at the Western Wall (7 June 1967)
sources.caption: David Rubinger's photograph of Israeli paratroopers (Zion Karasenti, Yitzhak Yifat, and Haim Oshri) standing in awe before the Western Wall in the captured Old City of Jerusalem, 7 June 1967.
sources.context: On 7 June 1967, Israeli paratroopers captured the Old City of Jerusalem and reached the Western Wall.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office / David Rubinger (GPO D1-1967), 7 June 1967.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the capture of the Old City and the Western Wall transform Israeli public attitudes from existential dread to religious and national euphoria?
discussion_ideas: Source E is exceptionally useful because it captures the raw emotional transition from the mortal dread of annihilation preceding June 5 to an overwhelming sense of miraculous historical vindication, cementing national attachment to the newly captured territories.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.3 Enquiry: "Land for Peace" or Permanent Stalemate: How Did the 1967 Conquered Territories Transform the Conflict?
sources.title: Source A: CIA Intelligence Map of Occupied Territories (1967)
sources.caption: Central Intelligence Agency secret situation map detailing Israeli military occupation zones, strategic passes, and Syrian ceasefire lines, July 1967.
sources.context: CIA intelligence analysts mapped the new ceasefire lines following the Six-Day War.
sources.provenance: National Archives and Records Administration, College Park (RG 263 / CIA-RDP84), July 1967.
sources.hinge_question: Why did US intelligence analysts conclude that Israeli control of the Golan and West Bank made an immediate peace settlement unlikely?
discussion_ideas: Source A is exceptionally useful because it provides an objective intelligence breakdown of the formidable geographical barriers—the Jordan River, Golan escarpment, and Suez Canal—that insulated Israeli population centers from sudden ground attack.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.3 Enquiry: "Land for Peace" or Permanent Stalemate: How Did the 1967 Conquered Territories Transform the Conflict?
sources.title: Source B: Military Governorate Administration Map of the West Bank (1968)
sources.caption: Israeli military command map detailing the administrative sub-districts (Jenin, Nablus, Ramallah, Hebron) placed under direct IDF military decree following Order No. 1.
sources.context: The IDF established military rule over the West Bank, issuing military orders to govern civil and security affairs.
sources.provenance: Israel Defense Forces Military Advocate General Archives, Tel Aviv, 1968.
sources.hinge_question: How did the imposition of Israeli military orders replace Jordanian civil law and reshape daily Palestinian life?
discussion_ideas: Source B indicates that Israel quickly moved from ad-hoc wartime policing to a highly organized, institutionalized military administration capable of maintaining long-term control over a hostile civilian population indefinitely.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.3 Enquiry: "Land for Peace" or Permanent Stalemate: How Did the 1967 Conquered Territories Transform the Conflict?
sources.title: Source C: Official Scanned Record of UN Security Council Resolution 242 (22 November 1967)
sources.caption: Facsimile of the official United Nations Security Council Record for Resolution 242 (S/RES/242), showing the bilingual English and French texts that established the fundamental 'Land for Peace' formula.
sources.context: UN Resolution 242 established the fundamental 'Land for Peace' formula.
sources.provenance: United Nations Security Council Official Records (S/RES/242), November 1967.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the deliberate omission of the definite article 'the' in the English version ('withdrawal from territories occupied') provoke perpetual diplomatic conflict?
discussion_ideas: Lord Caradon deliberately crafted constructive ambiguity so that both Israel (which refused to return to indefensible 1967 borders) and Arab states (demanding total evacuation of sovereign land) could sign without formally conceding their core demands.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.3 Enquiry: "Land for Peace" or Permanent Stalemate: How Did the 1967 Conquered Territories Transform the Conflict?
sources.title: Source D: The Bar Lev Line Fortress Fortifications on the Suez Canal (1969–1973)
sources.caption: Tactical map and engineering plan of the Bar-Lev Line fortifications along the eastern bank of the Suez Canal, showing fortified Maoz strongpoints and observation bunkers.
sources.context: Israel built the Bar Lev Line along the Suez Canal to fortify its defense during the War of Attrition.
sources.provenance: IDF Combat Engineering Corps / Ministry of Defense Archives, Tel Aviv, 1969.
sources.hinge_question: How did Israeli reliance on the massive physical ramparts of the Bar Lev Line breed dangerous military complacency (the 'Conception') before 1973?
discussion_ideas: Source D shows a static, heavily fortified Maginot-style defensive barrier that Israeli intelligence believed was unassailable, explaining why the IDF was completely stunned when Egyptian forces breached it with high-pressure water cannons in just six hours.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.3 Enquiry: "Land for Peace" or Permanent Stalemate: How Did the 1967 Conquered Territories Transform the Conflict?
sources.title: Source E: Strategic Cartographic Map of the Allon Plan (1967–1968)
sources.caption: Historical map illustrating Labor Minister Yigal Allon's settlement strategy: annexing a 10–15km defensive perimeter along the Jordan River (blue) while returning Arab population centres (green) to Jordanian civil administration.
sources.context: Yigal Allon proposed establishing agricultural settlements along the Jordan Valley as a strategic security barrier.
sources.provenance: Israel Labor Party Archives, Beit Berl (Allon Papers), July 1968.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Israeli government choose to create 'facts on the ground' through settlements rather than formally annexing the West Bank?
discussion_ideas: Source E is highly reliable for demonstrating the security-first mindset of early Labor leaders, but it fails to anticipate how the later Likud government and religious movements like Gush Emunim would discard strategic security buffers in favor of ideological settlement across the entire biblical heartland.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.4: The Rise of Palestinian Resistance: The PLO, Black September & Munich (1968–1972)
sources.title: Source A: Yasser Arafat in Military Battle Fatigues (1969)
sources.caption: Yasser Arafat in military battle fatigues and checkered kaffiyeh during a diplomatic and military summit following the 1968 Battle of Karameh (1969).
sources.context: Yasser Arafat took leadership of the PLO in 1969, making armed struggle central to its mission.
sources.provenance: Palestinian National Authority Information Department / Gamma-Rapho, c. 1969.
sources.hinge_question: How did Arafat's consistent adoption of military uniform project the image of an active guerrilla warrior rather than a desk-bound diplomat?
discussion_ideas: Arafat deliberately cultivated the persona of an austere guerrilla commander to establish his authority over competing factional rivals and prove to Palestinian refugees that their liberation lay in self-reliant armed resistance rather than reliance on untrustworthy Arab monarchs.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.4: The Rise of Palestinian Resistance: The PLO, Black September & Munich (1968–1972)
sources.title: Source B: PFLP Guerrillas Blowing Up Airplanes at Dawson's Field (1970)
sources.caption: Three hijacked Western airliners (BOAC, Swissair, TWA) detonated by Marxist PFLP guerrillas on a desert airstrip in Jordan on 12 September 1970 after releasing 300 passengers.
sources.context: The PFLP hijacked commercial airliners to Dawson's Field in Jordan, challenging the authority of King Hussein.
sources.provenance: Associated Press / AP Images (700912089), 12 September 1970.
sources.hinge_question: How did dramatic international airliner hijackings by groups like the PFLP force the Palestinian cause into global consciousness?
discussion_ideas: Source B is profoundly useful because it captures the transition from conventional state warfare to international asymmetric terror spectacles designed to bypass Arab regimes and compel global media coverage of Palestinian grievances.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.4: The Rise of Palestinian Resistance: The PLO, Black September & Munich (1968–1972)
sources.title: Source C: Military Cartographic Operations Map of Black September, Jordan (September 1970)
sources.caption: Military situation map of Jordan during the September 1970 civil war, charting the clashes between the Jordanian Armed Forces and PLO fedayeen brigades across Amman, Irbid, and Jerash, alongside the repelled Syrian armored column invasion.
sources.context: In September 1970, King Hussein launched an all-out offensive against PLO forces in Jordan.
sources.provenance: Jordanian Armed Forces Historical Directorate / Royal Archives, Amman, 1971.
sources.hinge_question: Why did King Hussein perceive the armed PLO presence as an intolerable threat to the survival of the Hashemite monarchy?
discussion_ideas: Source C shows the violent military expulsion of PLO forces from Jordan, which directly caused thousands of armed militants to relocate into southern Lebanon, overwhelming Lebanon's fragile sectarian balance and provoking the 1975 civil war.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.4: The Rise of Palestinian Resistance: The PLO, Black September & Munich (1968–1972)
sources.title: Source D: Fatah Fedayeen Fighters on Parade in Lebanon (January 1979)
sources.caption: Uniformed Palestinian Fatah fedayeen fighters, wearing keffiyehs and military fatigues, marching with Palestinian flags in Lebanon following the PLO’s relocation from Jordan into southern Lebanon ('Fatahland').
sources.context: The PLO established a major armed base in southern Lebanon, launching cross-border attacks into northern Israel.
sources.provenance: IDF Northern Command Intelligence Directorate, Safed, 1972.
sources.hinge_question: How did the 1969 Cairo Agreement between Lebanon and the PLO compromise Lebanese state sovereignty in the south?
discussion_ideas: Source D is highly reliable regarding IDF intelligence assessments of rocket launch corridors; however, because it was produced to justify Israeli cross-border incursions into Lebanon, it emphasizes guerrilla infrastructure while minimizing the heavy collateral casualties inflicted on Lebanese civilians.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.4: The Rise of Palestinian Resistance: The PLO, Black September & Munich (1968–1972)
sources.title: Source E: Yasser Arafat Addressing the UN General Assembly (1974)
sources.caption: Yasser Arafat addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 13 November 1974, famously concluding: 'I come bearing an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun. Do not let the olive branch fall from my hand.'
sources.context: On 13 November 1974, Yasser Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly, securing international diplomatic standing.
sources.provenance: United Nations Photo Archives (UN Photo 128456), 13 November 1974.
sources.hinge_question: How did Arafat's speech signal a shift in PLO strategy from pure guerrilla warfare to international diplomatic recognition?
discussion_ideas: Source E demonstrates that the Palestinian national movement had successfully evolved from being treated merely as an anonymous humanitarian refugee problem into an internationally recognized sovereign political nation with legitimate claims to self-determination.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.5: The War of Attrition & The Yom Kippur War (1969–1973)
sources.title: Source A: Tactical Blueprint of Bar-Lev Line Fortifications Along the Suez Canal (1969–1970)
sources.caption: Tactical map and engineering plan of the Bar-Lev Line fortifications along the eastern bank of the Suez Canal, showing fortified Maoz strongpoints and observation bunkers.
sources.context: The Bar-Lev Line was built along the Suez Canal between 1968 and 1970 as a fortified defensive barrier.
sources.provenance: IDF Combat Engineering Corps / Ministry of Defense Archives, Tel Aviv, 1969.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Israeli military strategists believe the massive sand ramparts of the Bar-Lev Line made a surprise Egyptian crossing impossible?
discussion_ideas: Source A is exceptionally useful because it illustrates the IDF's reliance on static, heavily fortified concrete strongpoints and massive earthen barriers to deter Egyptian offensive actions and protect the Sinai buffer zone.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.5: The War of Attrition & The Yom Kippur War (1969–1973)
sources.title: Source B: President Sadat Reviewing Battle Plans in Center 10 Operations Room (6 October 1973)
sources.caption: President Anwar Sadat studying operational military charts in the Egyptian Armed Forces Center 10 Operations Room alongside War Minister Ahmad Ismail Ali and Chief of Staff Saad el-Shazly during the surprise attack, 6 October 1973.
sources.context: President Sadat planned a limited war to break the diplomatic stalemate and restore Arab pride.
sources.provenance: Egyptian Presidency Information Agency / Al-Ahram Archive, October 1973.
sources.hinge_question: How did Sadat's political objective differ from earlier Arab leaders who sought the total military destruction of Israel?
discussion_ideas: Source B accurately reflects Sadat's wartime role as Supreme Commander; however, as an official state photograph, it obscures his later strategic blunder in ordering Egyptian armor out from under their SAM missile umbrella on 14 October, which led to disastrous tank losses.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.5: The War of Attrition & The Yom Kippur War (1969–1973)
sources.title: Source C: Egyptian Troops Breaching the Bar Lev Line (October 1973)
sources.caption: Egyptian Second Army assault troops crossing the Suez Canal in rubber dinghies under heavy covering fire during the surprise attack on the afternoon of 6 October 1973.
sources.context: On 6 October 1973, Egypt launched the surprise attack, successfully crossing the Suez Canal and taking the Bar Lev Line.
sources.provenance: Egyptian Ministry of Defense / Al-Ahram Archive (Badr-73), 6 October 1973.
sources.hinge_question: How did the technological innovation of using German high-pressure water pumps neutralize Israel's massive sand barriers?
discussion_ideas: Source C is exceptionally useful because it provides vivid photographic testimony of the meticulous military planning and morale that allowed Egyptian infantry to breach an unassailable defensive obstacle, shattering Israel's myth of invincibility.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.5: The War of Attrition & The Yom Kippur War (1969–1973)
sources.title: Source D: Israeli Armor Crossing the Deversoir Pontoon Bridge (October 1973)
sources.caption: Israeli Patton and Centurion tanks crossing the Suez Canal onto the Egyptian mainland over Gillois amphibious pontoon bridges at Deversoir, October 1973.
sources.context: Operation Nickel Grass provided crucial US military supplies that sustained Israel's counter-offensive.
sources.provenance: Israel Defense Forces Archives / Ministry of Defense, October 1973.
sources.hinge_question: How did the US emergency airlift (Operation Nickel Grass) enable Israel to execute this massive counter-offensive?
discussion_ideas: Source D is highly useful because it reveals that military victory hinged on monumental combat engineering feats—towing pre-fabricated steel roller bridges under relentless artillery fire to establish an unbreakable supply bridgehead into Africa.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 2.5: The War of Attrition & The Yom Kippur War (1969–1973)
sources.title: Source E: Henry Kissinger Conferring with Golda Meir and Richard Nixon (November 1973)
sources.caption: Prime Minister Golda Meir conferring with US President Richard Nixon and Secretary of State Henry Kissinger in the White House Oval Office, November 1973.
sources.context: Henry Kissinger conducted shuttle diplomacy to negotiate ceasefires and disengagement agreements.
sources.provenance: White House Photo Office / Richard Nixon Presidential Library (NLN-WHPO-MP-E1748), 1 November 1973.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Kissinger prevent Israel from destroying the encircled Egyptian Third Army at the end of the war?
discussion_ideas: Kissinger sought to maintain a stalemate where neither side achieved total victory, thereby ending Soviet influence in Cairo, restoring American diplomatic hegemony, and nudging Sadat into bilateral negotiations with Washington and Israel.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.1: Diplomatic Negotiations: From Shuttle Diplomacy to Camp David, 1974–1979
sources.title: Source A: Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin (1978)
sources.caption: Menachem Begin, former underground Irgun commander and Likud Prime Minister who negotiated the historic peace agreement with Egypt, 1978.
sources.context: Likud Prime Minister Menachem Begin agreed to return the entire Sinai in exchange for a separate peace with Egypt.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office (GPO D1-1978), 1978.
sources.hinge_question: Why was a hardline nationalist like Begin capable of surrendering the entire Sinai when Labor leaders could not?
discussion_ideas: Source A indicates that Begin made painful territorial concessions in the non-biblical Sinai Peninsula specifically to split the Arab world and protect Israeli sovereignty over the biblically sacred heartland of Judea and Samaria.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.1: Diplomatic Negotiations: From Shuttle Diplomacy to Camp David, 1974–1979
sources.title: Source B: President Jimmy Carter Addressing Congress on Camp David (18 September 1978)
sources.caption: President Jimmy Carter delivering his historic address to a joint session of the United States Congress announcing the signing of the Camp David Accords, 18 September 1978.
sources.context: President Carter intervened extensively at Camp David to bridge differences between Sadat and Begin.
sources.provenance: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (LC-U9-36657), 18 September 1978.
sources.hinge_question: How did Jimmy Carter's personal mediation and persistence prevent the Camp David negotiations from collapsing?
discussion_ideas: Carter sought to secure bipartisan congressional approval and multi-billion-dollar foreign military aid packages for both Egypt and Israel, which were the crucial financial guarantees underpinning the peace agreement.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.1: Diplomatic Negotiations: From Shuttle Diplomacy to Camp David, 1974–1979
sources.title: Source C: The Camp David Accords Framework Document (September 1978)
sources.caption: Facsimile copy of the signed 'Framework for Peace in the Middle East' signed by Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin at Camp David on 17 September 1978.
sources.context: The Camp David Accords established a framework for Egyptian-Israeli peace and interim Palestinian autonomy.
sources.provenance: US National Archives, Washington D.C. (RG 59 / Department of State Treaties), September 1978.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the Palestinian autonomy framework in the Camp David Accords rejected by both the PLO and Jordan?
discussion_ideas: Source C is extremely reliable as an official primary legal text, demonstrating that while the bilateral treaty with Egypt was ironclad and binding, the Palestinian autonomy sections were deliberately vague, aspirational, and unenforceable without Palestinian representation.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.1: Diplomatic Negotiations: From Shuttle Diplomacy to Camp David, 1974–1979
sources.title: Source D: The Historic White House Lawn Peace Handshake (March 1979)
sources.caption: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat, US President Jimmy Carter, and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin joining hands on the South Lawn of the White House after signing the Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty on 26 March 1979.
sources.context: On 26 March 1979, Egypt and Israel signed the historic peace treaty on the White House lawn.
sources.provenance: Jimmy Carter Presidential Library (NAID 175653), 26 March 1979.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the bilateral treaty between Egypt and Israel denounced as betrayal by the PLO and wider Arab world?
discussion_ideas: Source D is exceptionally useful because it captures the monumental breakthrough of the first peace treaty between Israel and an Arab neighbor, fundamentally dismantling the Arab military coalition by removing Egypt—the largest Arab army—from future conflict.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.1: Diplomatic Negotiations: From Shuttle Diplomacy to Camp David, 1974–1979
sources.title: Source E: Official CIA Map of Sinai Demilitarized Security Zones (March 1979)
sources.caption: Official Central Intelligence Agency cartographic map detailing the phased withdrawal zones (Zones A, B, C, and D) and UN peacekeeping positions across the Sinai Peninsula under the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty.
sources.context: Israel completed its three-stage military withdrawal from Sinai in April 1982 under the terms of the treaty.
sources.provenance: Multinational Force and Observers (MFO) Archives / US Department of State, 1982.
sources.hinge_question: How did the deployment of the MFO international peacekeeping force guarantee the demilitarization of the Sinai?
discussion_ideas: Source E provides concrete territorial proof of 'Land for Peace' in practice, showing that when an Arab state agreed to full diplomatic recognition, demilitarized zones, and secure borders, Israel completely surrendered conquered territory.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.2: The Palestinian Issue: Lebanon, Sabra & Shatila, and the First Intifada, 1974–1993
sources.title: Source A: IDF Operation Peace for Galilee Campaign Map (June 1982)
sources.caption: Military map depicting the three-pronged Israeli invasion of Lebanon in June 1982, rapidly advancing far beyond the 40km buffer zone to encircle West Beirut.
sources.context: Israel invaded Lebanon in June 1982, rapidly expanding the operation to besiege West Beirut.
sources.provenance: IDF History Department / Ministry of Defense, Tel Aviv, 1982.
sources.hinge_question: How did Defense Minister Ariel Sharon mislead Prime Minister Begin and the Cabinet regarding the true military objectives in Lebanon?
discussion_ideas: Source A is highly useful because the operational arrows visually prove that the IDF advanced 100 kilometers directly into the capital city of an Arab state, revealing that the war was not a limited defensive operation but an aggressive political intervention.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.2: The Palestinian Issue: Lebanon, Sabra & Shatila, and the First Intifada, 1974–1993
sources.title: Source B: Defence Minister Ariel Sharon Overlooking West Beirut from IDF Observation Post (August 1982)
sources.caption: Israeli Defence Minister Ariel Sharon surveying West Beirut and surrounding refugee camp sectors from an IDF rooftop command post with military operational maps, August 1982.
sources.context: Between 16-18 September 1982, Christian Phalangist militias murdered hundreds of Palestinian civilians in Sabra and Shatila.
sources.provenance: Israel Commission of Inquiry into the Events at the Refugee Camps in Beirut (Kahan Commission Report), February 1983.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Kahan Commission find Defense Minister Ariel Sharon 'indirectly responsible' for the massacre?
discussion_ideas: The Commission published the maps to independently investigate the spatial sightlines and proximity of IDF command posts to the camps, establishing whether Israeli generals knew the slaughter was taking place and failed to intervene.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.2: The Palestinian Issue: Lebanon, Sabra & Shatila, and the First Intifada, 1974–1993
sources.title: Source C: Palestinian Youth Confronting IDF Troops During the First Intifada
sources.caption: Palestinian youths using slingshots to throw stones against Israeli armored vehicles in the Gaza Strip during the First Intifada (1987-1988).
sources.context: In December 1987, the First Intifada erupted across Gaza and the West Bank as a popular uprising.
sources.provenance: Associated Press / AP Images (871215012), December 1987.
sources.hinge_question: How did the visual contrast between stone-throwing youths and heavily armed soldiers reverse traditional international perceptions of the conflict?
discussion_ideas: Source C demonstrates that the uprising was driven by widespread, unarmed civilian youth rather than foreign guerrilla armies, making standard IDF heavy mechanized warfare ineffective and morally damaging under the glare of international television cameras.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.2: The Palestinian Issue: Lebanon, Sabra & Shatila, and the First Intifada, 1974–1993
sources.title: Source D: Original Clandestine UNLU Leaflet (Bayan No. 1) Calling for General Strike (8 January 1988)
sources.caption: Original mimeographed underground leaflet (Bayan No. 1) issued by the Unified National Leadership of the Uprising (UNLU) on 8 January 1988, directing nationwide merchant shutdowns, labor strikes, and popular committee solidarity.
sources.context: The Unified National Leadership of the Uprising (UNLU) coordinated the First Intifada through clandestine mimeographed circulars, enforcing general strikes and civic non-cooperation.
