sources.provenance: Birzeit University Digital Palestinian Archives (Awraq Collection #8777) / Palestinian Museum Digital Archive (PMDA), 8 January 1988.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the underground UNLU leaflets prove more effective at mobilizing the Palestinian population than orders from the exiled PLO leadership in Tunis?
discussion_ideas: Source D shows that the Intifada was organized as a disciplined, society-wide civil rebellion using underground mimeographed strike orders rather than conventional military forces; cross-referenced with the widespread street clashes in Source D, it demonstrates why Rabin realized that military force ('breaking bones') could not defeat a whole civilian population committed to total economic and civil non-cooperation.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.2: The Palestinian Issue: Lebanon, Sabra & Shatila, and the First Intifada, 1974–1993
sources.title: Source E: Armed PLO Fedayeen Guerrillas in Southern Lebanon (c. 1979)
sources.caption: Armed Palestinian guerrillas in military fatigues operating from southern Lebanese border strongholds, illustrating the PLO military presence that provoked Israel's 1982 invasion.
sources.context: Archival photograph showing armed Palestinian fedayeen fighters operating in southern Lebanon prior to the 1982 Israeli invasion.
sources.provenance: PLO Unified Information Office / French Press Agency (AFP), Beirut, c. 1979.
sources.hinge_question: How does Sharon's direct presence overlooking Beirut illustrate why Israeli critics accused him of fighting a personal war beyond the Cabinet's approved mandate?
discussion_ideas: Source E shows heavily armed PLO guerrilla units operating freely along the southern Lebanese border, demonstrating why Israeli leaders viewed the armed Palestinian presence as an unacceptable cross-border security threat to civilian settlements in northern Galilee.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.3: Attempts at a Solution: From the Oslo Accords to Oslo II, 1988–1995
sources.title: Source A: The Opening Plenary of the Madrid Peace Conference (30 October 1991)
sources.caption: Delegations from Israel, Syria, Lebanon, and a joint Jordanian-Palestinian delegation assembling at the Royal Palace of Madrid, co-chaired by US President George H.W. Bush and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.
sources.context: The Madrid Peace Conference in October 1991 brought Israeli and Arab leaders together for the first face-to-face negotiations.
sources.provenance: White House Photographic Collection / US National Archives, 30 October 1991.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the joint sponsorship of both the United States and the Soviet Union essential for bringing Arab and Israeli delegations together at Madrid?
discussion_ideas: Source A is profoundly useful because it captures the unprecedented visual evidence of Israeli, Arab, and superpower leaders assembled in a single diplomatic hall, proving that the end of the Cold War fundamentally dissolved decades of diplomatic boycott.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.3: Attempts at a Solution: From the Oslo Accords to Oslo II, 1988–1995
sources.title: Source B: Official Israeli-Palestinian Negotiating Map for Oslo II (1995)
sources.caption: Official diplomatic map signed by Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat at Taba, detailing initial phased IDF redeployments from Jenin, Nablus, Tulkarm, Qalqilya, Ramallah, and Bethlehem.
sources.context: Oslo II scheduled gradual Israeli redeployments while postponing core final-status issues.
sources.provenance: Israel State Archives / Palestinian Authority Ministry of Planning, Taba, September 1995.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Oslo process defer final status issues (Jerusalem, refugees, borders, settlements) to later negotiations rather than resolving them immediately?
discussion_ideas: Negotiators designed a multi-year phased redeployment to allow both societies to build mutual confidence through joint security coordination before tackling the existential questions of Jerusalem and Palestinian statehood.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.3: Attempts at a Solution: From the Oslo Accords to Oslo II, 1988–1995
sources.title: Source C: The Historic Oslo Handshake on the White House Lawn (1993)
sources.caption: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat shaking hands on the White House South Lawn, encouraged by President Bill Clinton, following the signing of the Oslo Declaration of Principles on 13 September 1993.
sources.context: On 13 September 1993, Israel and the PLO signed the Oslo Accord on the White House lawn.
sources.provenance: White House Photographic Office / William J. Clinton Presidential Library (P08392-05), 13 September 1993.
sources.hinge_question: Why was Yitzhak Rabin visibly hesitant before extending his hand to shake that of Yasser Arafat?
discussion_ideas: Source C is monumentally useful because it visually captures the historic paradigm shift whereby mortal enemies formally recognized each other's national existence, transforming the conflict from an existential zero-sum war into a negotiated bilateral peace process.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.3: Attempts at a Solution: From the Oslo Accords to Oslo II, 1988–1995
sources.title: Source D: The Oslo II Cartographic Division of the West Bank (1995)
sources.caption: Cartographic map illustrating the fragmentation of the West Bank into Areas A (full Palestinian civil and security control), B (Palestinian civil and joint Israeli security control), and C (exclusive Israeli control covering 60% of territory).
sources.context: The 1995 Oslo II Agreement divided the West Bank into Areas A, B, and C.
sources.provenance: United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA-OPT), Jerusalem, 1995.
sources.hinge_question: How did the division of the West Bank into disconnected enclaves in Areas A and B hinder the emergence of a viable independent Palestinian state?
discussion_ideas: Source D reveals that Palestinian administrative zones (Areas A and B) were cut into dozens of non-contiguous territorial islands completely encircled by Area C, ensuring that Israel retained absolute control over water, roads, airspace, and freedom of movement.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 2: Conflict in the Middle East, 1945-1995
sources.lessonTitle: KT 3.3: Attempts at a Solution: From the Oslo Accords to Oslo II, 1988–1995
sources.title: Source E: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin Debating the Oslo II Accord in the Knesset (5 October 1995)
sources.caption: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin addressing the Knesset chamber during the impassioned debate on the Oslo II Interim Agreement, 5 October 1995.
sources.context: Prime Minister Rabin defended the Oslo process in the Knesset, facing ferocious opposition from right-wing Israeli politicians.
sources.provenance: Israel Government Press Office (GPO D1-1995), 5 October 1995.
sources.hinge_question: How did right-wing rhetoric branding Rabin a 'traitor' and 'murderer' create the political climate that led to his assassination?
discussion_ideas: Source E is extremely reliable as an official parliamentary record showing that Rabin never envisioned a fully sovereign Palestinian state, but rather a demilitarized entity with limited powers, aiming to safeguard Israel's democratic and Jewish character without returning to 1967 borders.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Ideological Clash: Why could Capitalism and Communism never peacefully coexist?
sources.title: Source A (Archival Document & Address): Joseph Stalin’s Bolshoi Theatre Election Speech (9 February 1946)
sources.caption: Official transcript and portrait plate of Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin delivering his landmark election address to Moscow voters at the Bolshoi Theatre on 9 February 1946.
sources.context: Stalin’s Bolshoi speech shattered Western hopes that wartime cooperation would continue into peacetime. In Washington, Supreme Court Justice William O. Douglas described the address as 'The Declaration of World War Three,' prompting the US State Department to urgently demand diplomatic analysis. **Hinge Question:** Why did Western leaders interpret Stalin’s ideological speech as a direct military warning to the capitalist world?
sources.provenance: Delivered in person by Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin at the Bolshoi Theatre, Moscow, on 9 February 1946; broadcast across Soviet radio and published on page one of Pravda.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Western leaders interpret Stalin’s ideological speech as a direct military warning to the capitalist world?
discussion_ideas: Stalin claimed capitalist nations were locked into violent competition for foreign markets, requiring the Soviet Union to prioritize heavy industry and military readiness over civilian consumer goods.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Ideological Clash: Why could Capitalism and Communism never peacefully coexist?
sources.title: Source B (Ideological Foundational Plate): Vladimir Lenin on Democratic Centralism and the Vanguard Party (1920)
sources.caption: Vladimir Lenin addresses Red Army recruits in Moscow in May 1920, championing the iron discipline of the Bolshevik vanguard party over multi-party parliamentary debate.
sources.context: Lenin’s core text established the bedrock doctrine taught in every Soviet school and university. To Western observers, this text proved that communist states were ideologically committed to the violent destruction of capitalist democracies. **Hinge Question:** If Soviet leaders were educated on Lenin's doctrine of violent revolution, why was it difficult for Western democracies to trust Soviet promises of peace?
sources.provenance: Written in hiding by Vladimir Lenin in August–September 1917 on the eve of the Bolshevik October Revolution; compulsory reading for all Soviet Communist Party officials.
sources.hinge_question: If Soviet leaders were educated on Lenin's doctrine of violent revolution, why was it difficult for Western democracies to trust Soviet promises of peace?
discussion_ideas: Lenin believed workers on their own would settle for modest wage reforms; only an organized, elite vanguard party could seize state power and enforce the socialist transformation of society.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Ideological Clash: Why could Capitalism and Communism never peacefully coexist?
sources.title: Source C (Political Satire & Archival Metaphor): David Low, 'Someone is Watching' (Evening Standard, March 1946)
sources.caption: David Low’s celebrated editorial cartoon published in the London Evening Standard in March 1946, visualizing Churchill’s 'Iron Curtain' speech as an impenetrable steel wall sealing off Eastern Europe under Red Army guard while John Bull peeks underneath.
sources.context: David Low was widely regarded as the greatest political cartoonist of the 20th century. Here he visualizes Churchill's metaphor of the Iron Curtain, capturing the British public's growing dismay that wartime alliance with Russia had transformed into secretive hostility. **Hinge Question:** What visual symbols does the cartoonist use to show that the Soviet government was deliberately shutting itself off from the rest of the world?
sources.provenance: Drawn by New Zealand-born political cartoonist David Low and published in the London Evening Standard in March 1946, immediately following Churchill's Fulton address.
sources.hinge_question: What visual symbols does the cartoonist use to show that the Soviet government was deliberately shutting itself off from the rest of the world?
discussion_ideas: It illustrates Western alarm that Stalin was violently severing Eastern Europe from the democratic world, sealing millions behind an impenetrable barrier guarded by the Red Army.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Ideological Clash: Why could Capitalism and Communism never peacefully coexist?
sources.title: Source D (Diplomatic Intelligence Plate): George Kennan and the Moscow Embassy "Long Telegram" (22 February 1946)
sources.caption: Archival portrait of US diplomat George F. Kennan in 1947, whose 8,000-word confidential dispatch from Moscow laid the intellectual foundation for the US policy of containment.
sources.context: Kennan’s telegram circulated through the highest levels of the Truman administration. Kennan argued that traditional diplomacy would fail with Moscow because Soviet leaders needed external enemies to justify their own tyrannical rule at home. **Hinge Question:** How did Kennan's claim that Soviet power is 'highly sensitive to logic of force' persuade President Truman to adopt a policy of military containment?
sources.provenance: Drafted by George F. Kennan, Chargé d'Affaires at the US Embassy in Moscow, and telegraphed in top-secret cipher to Secretary of State James Byrnes in Washington on 22 February 1946.
sources.hinge_question: How did Kennan's claim that Soviet power is 'highly sensitive to logic of force' persuade President Truman to adopt a policy of military containment?
discussion_ideas: Kennan explained that Soviet power was driven by traditional Russian insecurity and Marxist dogma, leading Moscow to view capitalism as an incurable enemy that could only be stopped through unyielding counter-force.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Ideological Clash: Why could Capitalism and Communism never peacefully coexist?
sources.title: Source E (Ideological Propaganda Plate): Supreme Soviet Election Appeal to Industrial Workers (February 1946)
sources.caption: Official Soviet state propaganda poster for the February 1946 Supreme Soviet elections: 'Long live our teacher, our father, our leader Comrade Stalin!', rallying workers to reconstruct socialist industry.
sources.context: While Western observers saw Soviet elections as rubber-stamp shams, Soviet domestic propaganda relentlessly hammered home economic comparisons: emphasizing full employment and social welfare to contrast with memories of the 1930s Western Great Depression. **Hinge Question:** Why did Soviet propaganda focus so heavily on full employment and healthcare while completely ignoring the absence of political opposition?
sources.provenance: Published by the State Publishing House for Political Literature (Gospolitizdat), Moscow, February 1946; plastered on factory noticeboards and streetcars during the Supreme Soviet elections.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Soviet propaganda focus so heavily on full employment and healthcare while completely ignoring the absence of political opposition?
discussion_ideas: It portrays Stalin as the heroic protector of the working class, promising that collective state ownership guarantees full employment and healthcare without capitalist exploitation.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Yalta to Potsdam (1945): How did wartime allies become bitter rivals?
sources.title: Source A (Archival Summit Photograph): The Big Three Seated in the Courtyard of Livadia Palace, Yalta (February 1945)
sources.caption: British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin seated in the courtyard of Livadia Palace during the Yalta Conference (February 1945).
sources.context: This iconic photograph captures the delicate summit diplomacy of the Grand Alliance. Roosevelt looks noticeably frail (he died two months later), while Stalin appears confident on home territory. **Hinge Question:** Why was it far easier for these three leaders to agree on defeating Nazi Germany than on how Europe should be governed after the war?
sources.provenance: Official Allied conference photograph taken by an Army Signal Corps photographer on the patio of Livadia Palace, Yalta, Crimea, between 4 and 11 February 1945.
sources.hinge_question: Why was it far easier for these three leaders to agree on defeating Nazi Germany than on how Europe should be governed after the war?
discussion_ideas: While projecting wartime harmony, Roosevelt appears physically exhausted, Churchill looks anxious over European balance of power, and Stalin sits confident knowing the Red Army occupied Eastern Europe.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Yalta to Potsdam (1945): How did wartime allies become bitter rivals?
sources.title: Source B (Official Diplomatic Accord): Protocol of Proceedings of the Crimea (Yalta) Conference (11 February 1945)
sources.caption: Official facsimile plate of the Declaration on Liberated Europe signed at Yalta, guaranteeing free and democratic elections across war-torn Europe.
sources.context: This declaration was hailed in the West as a triumph for democracy. However, Stalin interpreted 'democratic' governments in Eastern Europe to mean governments that were unconditionally friendly and subservient to Moscow. **Hinge Question:** Why did Stalin's definition of 'democracy' in Poland completely contradict what Churchill and Roosevelt expected when they signed this declaration?
sources.provenance: Jointly drafted and signed by Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill at Livadia Palace, Yalta, on 11 February 1945.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Stalin's definition of 'democracy' in Poland completely contradict what Churchill and Roosevelt expected when they signed this declaration?
discussion_ideas: They pledged to assist liberated populations in forming broadly representative interim governments and holding free, democratic elections as early as possible.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Yalta to Potsdam (1945): How did wartime allies become bitter rivals?
sources.title: Source C (Diplomatic Confrontation Plate): President Truman, Premier Stalin, and Foreign Minister Molotov (July 1945)
sources.caption: President Harry S. Truman, Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin, and Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov conferring at Cecilienhof Palace during the Potsdam Conference (July 1945).
sources.context: Unlike the diplomatic Roosevelt, Truman was blunt and combative. Having received news of the successful Trinity atomic bomb test just hours earlier, Truman was determined to halt Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe. **Hinge Question:** Did Truman's aggressive, no-nonsense style trigger Soviet paranoia, or was Stalin already planning to dominate Eastern Europe regardless of who was US president?
sources.provenance: Delivered orally by President Harry S. Truman at the opening plenary session of the Potsdam Conference in Cecilienhof Palace, Germany, 17 July 1945.
sources.hinge_question: Did Truman's aggressive, no-nonsense style trigger Soviet paranoia, or was Stalin already planning to dominate Eastern Europe regardless of who was US president?
discussion_ideas: Truman directly confronted Molotov over Soviet violations of the Yalta agreements in Poland, insisting that diplomatic agreements were a two-way street and refusing to tolerate Soviet stalling.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Yalta to Potsdam (1945): How did wartime allies become bitter rivals?
sources.title: Source D (Nuclear Turning Point): The Atomic Bomb and Truman’s Potsdam Calculations (July–August 1945)
sources.caption: The towering mushroom cloud rising above Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, providing horrific confirmation of the atomic monopoly Truman had learned about while conferring with Stalin at Potsdam.
sources.context: This deeply personal diary entry shows Truman grappling with the terrifying moral weight of atomic weaponry while simultaneously realizing that it gave America supreme geopolitical supremacy over Stalin. **Hinge Question:** Truman wrote that the atomic bomb might be 'the most terrible thing ever discovered.' Why did he still choose to drop it on Hiroshima and Nagasaki two weeks later?
sources.provenance: Written by President Harry S. Truman in his private bedside journal at the 'Little White House' in Babelsberg, near Potsdam, Germany, on 25 July 1945.
sources.hinge_question: Truman wrote that the atomic bomb might be 'the most terrible thing ever discovered.' Why did he still choose to drop it on Hiroshima and Nagasaki two weeks later?
discussion_ideas: It convinced Truman that the US no longer needed Soviet military assistance to defeat Japan, giving him immense diplomatic leverage to resist Soviet demands for German reparations.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Yalta to Potsdam (1945): How did wartime allies become bitter rivals?
sources.title: Source E (Archival Protocol Plate): Churchill, Truman, and Stalin on the Terrace of Cecilienhof Palace (Potsdam, July 1945)
sources.caption: Clement Attlee, Harry S. Truman, and Joseph Stalin meeting on the terrace of Cecilienhof Palace, Potsdam, establishing the quadripartite division and demilitarisation of Germany.
sources.context: While the Potsdam Agreement mandated that Germany be treated as a 'single economic unit,' the four powers (US, USSR, Britain, France) each administered their own zones completely differently. Stalin systematically stripped his Eastern zone of industrial machinery as reparations, setting the stage for the permanent division of Germany. **Hinge Question:** Why did the pledge to treat Germany as a 'single economic unit' fail within months of signing this agreement?
sources.provenance: Formally signed by Premier Joseph Stalin, President Harry S. Truman, and Prime Minister Clement Attlee at Cecilienhof Palace, Potsdam, on 2 August 1945.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the pledge to treat Germany as a 'single economic unit' fail within months of signing this agreement?
discussion_ideas: The Allies agreed to completely demilitarise Germany, dissolve all Nazi institutions, and extract reparations primarily from each occupying power’s own administrative zone.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: The Iron Curtain & The Berlin Blockade (1948–1949): The first flashpoint.
sources.title: Source A (Archival Speech Manuscript): Winston Churchill’s "Sinews of Peace" Reading Copy (Fulton, 5 March 1946)
sources.caption: Facsimile of the reading copy of Winston Churchill’s historic address at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, coining the defining phrase of the Cold War.
sources.context: Churchill was now the leader of the opposition in Britain. Free from diplomatic office, he used his speech to issue a direct warning to the American people that Stalin had betrayed his wartime promises and was turning Eastern Europe into a prison of communist police states. **Hinge Question:** Why did Soviet newspapers immediately attack Churchill as a 'warmonger' following this speech?
sources.provenance: Delivered in person by former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, on 5 March 1946, with President Harry S. Truman seated beside him on the platform.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Soviet newspapers immediately attack Churchill as a 'warmonger' following this speech?
discussion_ideas: Churchill warned that Moscow had imposed total military, political, and police control across Eastern and Central Europe, completely cutting those captive nations off from Western democratic contact.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: The Iron Curtain & The Berlin Blockade (1948–1949): The first flashpoint.
sources.title: Source B (Official Address to Congress): President Truman Delivering the "Truman Doctrine" Speech (12 March 1947)
sources.caption: President Harry S. Truman addresses a joint session of the United States Congress on 12 March 1947, requesting $400 million in emergency military aid for Greece and Turkey to contain Soviet expansion.
sources.context: Britain had informed Washington that it could no longer afford to fund the royalist Greek government fighting communist guerrillas. Truman seized the moment to announce an open-ended American commitment to intervene globally to stop the spread of communism. **Hinge Question:** Was the Truman Doctrine a noble defense of human freedom, or an aggressive American pledge to police the entire globe?
sources.provenance: Delivered in person by President Harry S. Truman before a joint session of the United States Congress on 12 March 1947.
sources.hinge_question: Was the Truman Doctrine a noble defense of human freedom, or an aggressive American pledge to police the entire globe?
discussion_ideas: Truman declared that America had a moral and strategic duty to support free peoples who were resisting attempted subjugation by armed communist minorities or outside foreign pressures.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: The Iron Curtain & The Berlin Blockade (1948–1949): The first flashpoint.
sources.title: Source C (Cartographic Operational Map): Allied Flight Corridors into Blockaded West Berlin (1948–1949)
sources.caption: Official cartographic plan showing the three narrow 20-mile-wide air corridors crossing 110 miles of Soviet-occupied East Germany from Hamburg, Bückeburg, and Frankfurt into West Berlin.
sources.context: When Stalin cut all road, canal, and railway connections to West Berlin on 24 June 1948, the Allies only had a written agreement guaranteeing air access. This map dictated the flight path for over 278,000 transport sorties. **Hinge Question:** Why did Stalin stop all road and rail traffic into Berlin, but deliberately avoid shooting down Allied transport planes in these air corridors?
sources.provenance: Drawn by Allied Air Safety Center navigators in Berlin, June 1948, establishing the designated flight corridors (Northern Corridor from Hamburg, Central Corridor from Bueckeburg/Hanover, Southern Corridor from Frankfurt).
sources.hinge_question: Why did Stalin stop all road and rail traffic into Berlin, but deliberately avoid shooting down Allied transport planes in these air corridors?
discussion_ideas: Any aircraft drifting outside the strict 20-mile boundary faced Soviet fighter buzzing or anti-aircraft radar tracking, requiring flights every three minutes in all weather conditions.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: The Iron Curtain & The Berlin Blockade (1948–1949): The first flashpoint.
sources.title: Source D (Humanitarian Archival Plate): Lieutenant Gail Halvorsen and German Children during "Operation Little Vittles" (1948)
sources.caption: US Air Force transport pilot Lieutenant Gail Halvorsen, the famous "Candy Bomber", ties miniature parachutes containing chocolate bars and chewing gum to drop to Berlin children waiting near Tempelhof Airport.
sources.context: During the 11-month blockade, Allied aircraft landed every 90 seconds, delivering over 2.3 million tons of flour, coal, and medicine. Lieutenant Gail Halvorsen began dropping candy bars attached to tiny handkerchief parachutes for Berlin children, turning a military standoff into an immense humanitarian propaganda victory. **Hinge Question:** How did the Berlin Airlift transform how ordinary Germans viewed American and British soldiers—from wartime conquerors into protectors?
sources.provenance: Photographed by a US Air Force combat camera crew at Tempelhof Airport, West Berlin, autumn 1948; widely published in Life magazine and European newspapers.
sources.hinge_question: How did the Berlin Airlift transform how ordinary Germans viewed American and British soldiers—from wartime conquerors into protectors?
discussion_ideas: It transformed former wartime bombing enemies into compassionate protectors in the eyes of German civilians, winning the psychological and moral battle of the Cold War.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: The Iron Curtain & The Berlin Blockade (1948–1949): The first flashpoint.
sources.title: Source E (Treaty Signing Facsimile): President Truman and Foreign Ministers Signing the North Atlantic Treaty (4 April 1949)
sources.caption: Foreign ministers of twelve founding nations sign the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, D.C. on 4 April 1949, establishing NATO and codifying Article 5 collective defence.
sources.context: The Berlin Blockade convinced Western leaders that Stalin was prepared to use force to expand his empire. NATO was created to link American nuclear power directly to the defense of Western Europe. **Hinge Question:** Why was signing Article 5 such a historic turning point for the United States, which had avoided permanent European military alliances for 150 years?
sources.provenance: Signed by the foreign ministers of twelve founding nations (including the US, UK, France, Canada, and the Netherlands) in Washington, D.C., on 4 April 1949.
sources.hinge_question: Why was signing Article 5 such a historic turning point for the United States, which had avoided permanent European military alliances for 150 years?
discussion_ideas: Under Article 5, all twelve nations agreed that an armed attack against one member in Europe or North America would be considered an attack against them all, pledging immediate collective military defence.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Nuclear Brinkmanship: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
sources.title: Source A (Aerial Reconnaissance Plate): Declassified CIA U-2 Spy Flight Photo of San Cristóbal, Cuba (14 October 1962)
sources.caption: High-altitude reconnaissance photograph taken by Major Richard Heyser flying a Lockheed U-2 over San Cristóbal, showing Soviet medium-range ballistic missile trailers and launch pads under construction.
sources.context: This photograph triggered the Cuban Missile Crisis. NPIC analysts proved that Soviet technicians were constructing launch pads capable of targeting Washington, D.C., New York, and major US cities within minutes. **Hinge Question:** Why did Soviet missiles placed in Cuba pose a far greater psychological and military threat to America than missiles based inside Russia?
sources.provenance: Captured by high-altitude camera aboard a USAF / CIA U-2 reconnaissance aircraft on 14 October 1962; analyzed by the National Photographic Interpretation Center (NPIC) in Washington.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Soviet missiles placed in Cuba pose a far greater psychological and military threat to America than missiles based inside Russia?
discussion_ideas: Photo analysts identified missile canvas covers, oxidizer trailers, and concrete bunkers matching the exact footprint of Soviet R-12 medium-range ballistic missile bases in the USSR.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Nuclear Brinkmanship: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
sources.title: Source B (Political Satire & Metaphor): Leslie Illingworth, 'The Arm-Wrestle' (Daily Mail, 29 October 1962)
sources.caption: Leslie Gilbert Illingworth’s celebrated editorial cartoon published on 29 October 1962, depicting Kennedy and Khrushchev locked in an agonizing arm-wrestle atop hydrogen bombs with their fingers on the detonator buttons.
sources.context: Illingworth perfectly captured the concept of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD). Both Kennedy and Khrushchev were trapped by their own military arsenals; pushing for victory meant total annihilation for both. **Hinge Question:** Why does the cartoonist show both leaders sweating with their fingers hovering over the detonator buttons?
sources.provenance: Drawn by British satirical artist Leslie Illingworth and published in Punch magazine on 29 October 1962, the very day the crisis was resolved.
sources.hinge_question: Why does the cartoonist show both leaders sweating with their fingers hovering over the detonator buttons?
discussion_ideas: The cartoonist warns that pushing for total military victory in the arm-wrestle would instantly trigger nuclear annihilation for both leaders, illustrating the terrifying reality of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD).

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Nuclear Brinkmanship: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
sources.title: Source C (Archival Audio & Broadcast Address): President John F. Kennedy’s Address on the Cuban Missile Crisis (22 October 1962)
sources.caption: President John F. Kennedy delivers his live television and radio address to the American people from the Oval Office on 22 October 1962, publicly announcing the discovery of Soviet missile sites in Cuba and declaring a naval quarantine.
sources.context: Kennedy had concealed the crisis for six days while debating secretly with his Executive Committee (ExComm). This address informed an astonished world that nuclear armageddon was suddenly imminent. **Hinge Question:** General Curtis LeMay urged Kennedy to immediately bomb the missile sites. Why did Kennedy resist military pressure and choose a naval quarantine instead?
sources.provenance: Broadcast live to the world from the Oval Office, Washington, D.C., on Monday evening, 22 October 1962.
sources.hinge_question: General Curtis LeMay urged Kennedy to immediately bomb the missile sites. Why did Kennedy resist military pressure and choose a naval quarantine instead?
discussion_ideas: By broadcasting directly to global citizens, Kennedy created overwhelming public pressure on Moscow, rallied NATO and Latin American allies, and demonstrated America’s unwavering resolve to block Soviet nuclear aggression.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Nuclear Brinkmanship: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
sources.title: Source D (Diplomatic Statecraft Facsimile): Draft of President Kennedy’s Confidential Letter to Premier Khrushchev (24 October 1962)
sources.caption: Declassified archival draft of President Kennedy’s urgent personal letter to Nikita Khrushchev, demanding that Soviet ships halt and warning against triggering an uncontrollable catastrophe.
sources.context: This remarkable letter revealed to Kennedy that Khrushchev was terrified of the crisis spiraling out of control. It opened the diplomatic path that allowed both sides to reach a face-saving compromise. **Hinge Question:** Does Khrushchev’s emotional, unedited letter show a dangerous dictator backing down, or a terrified human being desperate to prevent a nuclear apocalypse?
sources.provenance: Dictated by Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev in Moscow on the evening of 26 October 1962 and cabled urgently in cipher to the Soviet Embassy in Washington for delivery to JFK.
sources.hinge_question: Does Khrushchev’s emotional, unedited letter show a dangerous dictator backing down, or a terrified human being desperate to prevent a nuclear apocalypse?
discussion_ideas: Khrushchev warned that escalating military ultimatums would pull the knot so tight that neither leader would be able to untie it, leaving war as the only horrific outcome.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Nuclear Brinkmanship: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
sources.title: Source E (Heroism from Below): Soviet Submarine B-59 and Flotilla Chief of Staff Vasili Arkhipov (October 1962)
sources.caption: Archival plate of Foxtrot-class Soviet submarine B-59 surfaced near Cuba. Trapped under depth charges, Brigade Chief of Staff Vasili Arkhipov refused to authorize firing its nuclear torpedo, averting World War III.
sources.context: Submarine B-59 was armed with a 10-kiloton nuclear torpedo. Cut off from Moscow and suffering from blistering 50°C cabin heat and battery failure, Captain Savitsky and Political Officer Maslennikov both voted to launch the nuclear weapon, believing World War III had already begun. Brigade Chief of Staff **Vasili Arkhipov** used his veto power to refuse authorization, single-handedly preventing a nuclear exchange. **Hinge Question:** How does Arkhipov's story prove that the world was saved from nuclear war not just by presidents in Washington and Moscow, but by the courage of one individual officer?
sources.provenance: Photographed by a US Navy reconnaissance aircraft on 28 October 1962 as B-59 surfaced to recharge batteries. Testimony recorded at the Havana 40th Anniversary Conference (2002).
sources.hinge_question: How does Arkhipov's story prove that the world was saved from nuclear war not just by presidents in Washington and Moscow, but by the courage of one individual officer?
discussion_ideas: Suffocating in extreme heat and cut off from Moscow, Arkhipov stood alone against the submarine captain and political officer, knowing a nuclear launch would doom humanity.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Proxy Wars: Why did the superpowers fight in Asia (Korea & Vietnam)?
sources.title: Source A (Grand Strategy Directive): Declassified Cover of National Security Council Report NSC-68 (14 April 1950)
sources.caption: Official declassified title page of NSC-68, the top-secret national security directive authored by Paul Nitze that militarized American Cold War containment across the globe.
sources.context: NSC-68 transformed US foreign policy from regional containment in Europe into a militarized global crusade. Two months after it was signed, North Korea invaded South Korea, convincing Washington that Moscow was launching its global military offensive. **Hinge Question:** Did the 'Domino Theory' accurately describe the spread of Asian communism, or did it blind American leaders to local struggles for national independence?
sources.provenance: Drafted by Paul Nitze and the Policy Planning Staff, presented to President Truman on 14 April 1950; classified Top Secret until declassified in 1975.
sources.hinge_question: Did the 'Domino Theory' accurately describe the spread of Asian communism, or did it blind American leaders to local struggles for national independence?
discussion_ideas: NSC-68 argued the Soviet Union was driven by a fanatical ambition for world domination, meaning a communist advance in Asia or Africa weakened America’s global security perimeter.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Proxy Wars: Why did the superpowers fight in Asia (Korea & Vietnam)?
sources.title: Source C (Battlefield Medicine & Diary Plate): Frontline Medical Evacuation and Battlefield Trauma in Vietnam (1966)
sources.caption: Combat medical corpsmen treat severe battlefield blast wounds under fire in South Vietnam, mirroring the tragic frontline diary accounts kept by wartime medics like Dr. Đặng Thùy Trâm.
sources.context: Dr. Trâm’s diary was saved from burning by an American intelligence officer who was told by his translator: 'Do not burn this, it already has fire in it.' It gives an extraordinary, deeply human voice to the Vietnamese fighters who endured relentless American bombing. **Hinge Question:** How does reading a young Vietnamese doctor’s private diary challenge the one-sided view of the Vietnam War often shown in Western movies?
sources.provenance: Written in a pocket notebook in an underground bunker hospital in Quảng Ngãi Province, 1968; captured by US soldiers in 1970 and preserved by military intelligence.
sources.hinge_question: How does reading a young Vietnamese doctor’s private diary challenge the one-sided view of the Vietnam War often shown in Western movies?
discussion_ideas: They document horrific civilian and soldier casualties, severe shrapnel wounds, and the deep sorrow of watching teenage fighters die in makeshift jungle aid stations.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Proxy Wars: Why did the superpowers fight in Asia (Korea & Vietnam)?
sources.title: Source D (Guerrilla Warfare Tactics Plate): Subterranean Warfare: US Engineer 'Tunnel Rat' Entering Viet Cong Tunnel Complex (1967)
sources.caption: A US Army combat engineer 'tunnel rat' armed with a flashlight and pistol prepares to descend into a concealed trapdoor of the vast Củ Chi subterranean guerrilla tunnel network during Operation Cedar Falls (1967).
sources.context: The helicopter defined the Vietnam War. Over 7,000 Hueys were deployed to airlift troops into inaccessible jungles, evacuate the wounded within minutes, and deliver massive firepower. **Hinge Question:** The US military flew over 36 million helicopter sorties in Vietnam. Why was overwhelming technological mobility still not enough to win the war?
sources.provenance: Photographed by an official US Army combat photographer during an airmobile assault operation in Binh Dinh Province, South Vietnam, 1966.
sources.hinge_question: The US military flew over 36 million helicopter sorties in Vietnam. Why was overwhelming technological mobility still not enough to win the war?
discussion_ideas: The subterranean tunnels allowed Viet Cong guerrillas to vanish underground beneath US artillery and air strikes, launch surprise ambushes at point-blank range, and safely store ammunition and medical supplies.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Proxy Wars: Why did the superpowers fight in Asia (Korea & Vietnam)?
sources.title: Source E (Strategic Military Map): Nationwide Strikes of the Tet Offensive and the Ho Chi Minh Trail (1968)
sources.caption: Strategic theatre map plotting the coordinated Viet Cong and North Vietnamese assault across 100 cities, towns, and provincial capitals during the lunar new year holiday of Tet in January 1968.
sources.context: On 31 January 1968, during the Vietnamese lunar new year (Tet), over 80,000 communist troops launched coordinated surprise attacks across South Vietnam, even breaching the US Embassy in Saigon. While militarily crushed by US firepower, Tet shattered the American public's belief that victory was near. **Hinge Question:** The US military defeated the Viet Cong militarily during Tet. Why was the offensive still considered a catastrophic political and psychological defeat for the United States?
sources.provenance: Compiled by military historians at the Department of History, United States Military Academy at West Point, from declassified MACV combat logs.
sources.hinge_question: The US military defeated the Viet Cong militarily during Tet. Why was the offensive still considered a catastrophic political and psychological defeat for the United States?
discussion_ideas: It proved that despite years of bombing and over 500,000 US troops deployed, the communist forces retained the capability to strike every major urban centre in the country simultaneously.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the collapse of the Soviet Union (1991).
sources.title: Source A (Archival Confrontation Photo): US and Soviet Tanks Facing Off at Checkpoint Charlie, Berlin (October 1961)
sources.caption: American M48 Patton tanks and Soviet T-54 tanks stand gun-barrel to gun-barrel just 100 yards apart at Checkpoint Charlie on Friedrichstraße during the tense 16-hour standoff of 27–28 October 1961.
sources.context: Following the building of the Berlin Wall in August 1961, a dispute over whether East German police could check the passports of US diplomats led to armed tanks deploying with live ammunition. For 16 hours, the world stood on the brink of World War III until Kennedy and Khrushchev privately agreed to pull back one tank at a time. **Hinge Question:** Why did the Soviet Union and East Germany feel forced to build a concrete wall across Berlin to stop their own citizens from leaving?
sources.provenance: Photographed by US Army Signal Corps photographers stationed at Checkpoint Charlie, Berlin, on 28 October 1961.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Soviet Union and East Germany feel forced to build a concrete wall across Berlin to stop their own citizens from leaving?
discussion_ideas: The tanks stood within point-blank range with engines running and live shells loaded, meaning an accidental shot by a single nervous soldier could have escalated into global war.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the collapse of the Soviet Union (1991).
sources.title: Source B (Border Partition Plate): East German Troops Stringing Barbed Wire Along Bernauer Straße (August 1961)
sources.caption: East German combat police (Kampfgruppen) and border soldiers unroll coils of barbed wire and erect cinder-block barriers along Bernauer Straße in August 1961 to seal off West Berlin.
sources.context: Between 1949 and 1961, over 2.7 million East Germans (mostly young professionals, doctors, and engineers) fled to the West through Berlin. In 'Operation Rose', East German leader Walter Ulbricht sealed the border in a single night. **Hinge Question:** The East German government called the wall an 'Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart.' Who were the machine guns and watchtowers really pointing at?
sources.provenance: Handwritten in a private personal diary in East Berlin on 13 August 1961; preserved in family records and donated to the Berlin Wall Memorial Archive.
sources.hinge_question: The East German government called the wall an 'Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart.' Who were the machine guns and watchtowers really pointing at?
discussion_ideas: It shows soldiers abruptly tearing apart a peaceful city street with razor wire and armed guards, severing families, cutting off jobs, and trapping relatives on opposite sides overnight.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the collapse of the Soviet Union (1991).
sources.title: Source C (Economic Stagnation & Everyday Scarcity): Soviet Shoppers Facing Chronic Shortages in Moscow (c. 1980s)
sources.caption: Soviet women shopping for shoes in a state-run Moscow department store, examining sparse, low-quality footwear amidst the pervasive consumer shortages of the late Brezhnev and Gorbachev eras.
sources.context: By 1980, the Soviet economy was stagnating. While the USSR matched America in nuclear warheads and space exploration, its planned economy was incapable of producing basic consumer goods, forcing citizens to spend hours queuing for shoes, toilet paper, and meat. **Hinge Question:** Why did the Soviet command economy excel at building nuclear missiles and space rockets, but completely fail at providing shoes, toilet paper, and cars for its people?
sources.provenance: Published by Pravda Publishing House in Krokodil, the official state-authorized satirical weekly of the Soviet Union, circulation 5 million copies.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Soviet command economy excel at building nuclear missiles and space rockets, but completely fail at providing shoes, toilet paper, and cars for its people?
discussion_ideas: Citizens grew cynical and exhausted seeing that while the state poured vast resources into nuclear missiles, it could not supply basic shoes, meat, or apartments to ordinary working families.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the collapse of the Soviet Union (1991).
sources.title: Source D (Turning Point Press Conference): Günter Schabowski Announcing the Opening of the Berlin Border (9 November 1989)
sources.caption: East German Politburo spokesman Günter Schabowski answers questions at the international press conference in East Berlin on 9 November 1989, inadvertently triggering the fall of the Berlin Wall by stating new travel regulations took effect "immediately, without delay."
sources.context: For 28 years, the Berlin Wall had stood as the ultimate symbol of totalitarian oppression. When crowds converged on the checkpoints on the night of 9 November 1989, border guards refused to shoot. The fall of the wall signaled the peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe. **Hinge Question:** Why did the East German border guards refuse to fire on the crowds on the night of 9 November 1989?
sources.provenance: Photographed on the morning of 10 November 1989 as border checkpoints were overwhelmed following Günter Schabowski's accidental announcement of free travel.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the East German border guards refuse to fire on the crowds on the night of 9 November 1989?
discussion_ideas: When asked when the new travel rules took effect, Schabowski mistakenly answered 'immediately, without delay,' causing thousands of East Berliners to rush checkpoints and overwhelm bewildered border guards who yielded and opened the gates.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the collapse of the Soviet Union (1991).
sources.title: Source E (Imperial Dissolution Plate): Mikhail Gorbachev Delivering Farewell Address in the Kremlin (25 December 1991)
sources.caption: President Mikhail Gorbachev delivers his televised resignation address from the Kremlin on 25 December 1991, announcing the formal dissolution of the Soviet Union after 69 years.
sources.context: Gorbachev had sought to save socialism through reform (*Glasnost* and *Perestroika*), not destroy it. His refusal to use military violence to hold the Soviet empire together allowed 15 new independent nations to emerge peacefully. **Hinge Question:** Did Gorbachev's reforms destroy the Soviet Union, or was the communist system already doomed by economic failure and the arms race?
sources.provenance: Broadcast live across Soviet television from his office in the Kremlin, Moscow, at 7:00 PM on 25 December 1991; moments later, the red Soviet hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered forever.
sources.hinge_question: Did Gorbachev's reforms destroy the Soviet Union, or was the communist system already doomed by economic failure and the arms race?
discussion_ideas: Gorbachev took pride in dismantling totalitarian terror, guaranteeing democratic freedoms, halting the nuclear arms race, and integrating Russia peacefully into the community of nations.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Assessment: Was the Cold War ever truly 'cold'?
sources.title: Source A (Photographic Plate): The Castle Bravo 15-Megaton Thermonuclear Test, Bikini Atoll (1 March 1954)
sources.caption: Archival photograph of the mushroom cloud from Operation Castle Bravo, detonated on Bikini Atoll on 1 March 1954. Producing a 15-megaton blast—1,000 times more powerful than Hiroshima—it proved the catastrophic potential of hydrogen weaponry and accelerated superpower Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD).
sources.context: Archival photograph of the 15-megaton Castle Bravo thermonuclear detonation on Bikini Atoll, 1 March 1954. The hydrogen bomb ushered in the era of thermonuclear overkill and Mutual Assured Destruction. **Hinge Question:** Why did the terrifying destructive power of thermonuclear weapons like Castle Bravo paradoxically prevent the USA and USSR from ever engaging in direct military conflict?
sources.provenance: Official US military documentary photograph taken from an observation aircraft 50 miles away during Operation Castle Bravo, Marshall Islands, 1 March 1954.
sources.hinge_question: If having 500 nuclear bombs is enough to destroy human civilization, why did the two superpowers spend billions building over 60,000 warheads?
discussion_ideas: Source A reveals that the invention of thermonuclear weapons shifted superpower competition from atomic warfare to city-destroying megaton weapons. Castle Bravo was 1,000 times more destructive than the Hiroshima bomb, establishing the reality of Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD) where neither side could survive a nuclear war.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Assessment: Was the Cold War ever truly 'cold'?
sources.title: Source B (Civil Defence Archival Plate): British Government "Protect and Survive" Nuclear Guide (1980)
sources.caption: Official cover and instructional plate from the British Home Office public information booklet "Protect and Survive" (May 1980), advising families how to build improvised fallout rooms inside their homes.
sources.context: The booklet instructed ordinary British families to construct an 'inner core refuge' inside their homes by removing interior doors, leaning them against a wall at an angle, and piling heavy luggage and bags of earth on top. It sparked fierce public ridicule from peace campaigners (like CND and E.P. Thompson's *Protest and Survive*), who pointed out that domestic doors provided zero protection against a thermonuclear blast. **Hinge Question:** Did booklets like Protect and Survive give people genuine hope of surviving a nuclear war, or was it government propaganda to stop the public from panicking?
sources.provenance: Published by Her Majesty's Stationery Office (HMSO) on behalf of the British Home Office in May 1980; prepared for mass distribution to every British household.
sources.hinge_question: Did booklets like Protect and Survive give people genuine hope of surviving a nuclear war, or was it government propaganda to stop the public from panicking?
discussion_ideas: The booklet instructed civilians to wedge removed interior doors against walls and pack them with heavy suitcases, earth bags, and books to shield against deadly radioactive fallout.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Assessment: Was the Cold War ever truly 'cold'?
sources.title: Source C (Subterranean Bunker Plate): Blast Doors and Decontamination Lock, York Cold War Bunker
sources.caption: Heavy blast door and airlock entrance to the English Heritage subterranean Royal Observer Corps bunker in York, built to track nuclear fallout and coordinate government continuity.
sources.context: Beneath the suburbs of York lies a semi-sunken two-story concrete bunker. Sixty volunteer ROC observers would have been sealed inside for thirty days to plot nuclear bomb detonations, calculate radioactive fallout patterns, and broadcast the four-minute warning siren to the public. **Hinge Question:** Who was this bunker designed to protect, and what does that tell us about who the state valued most during a nuclear attack?
sources.provenance: Constructed in secret in 1961 by the British Home Office and Royal Observer Corps; preserved in original operational condition by English Heritage.
sources.hinge_question: Who was this bunker designed to protect, and what does that tell us about who the state valued most during a nuclear attack?
discussion_ideas: It reveals government recognition that surface survival was impossible, necessitating heavily shielded subterranean bunkers to keep military and administrative communications alive.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Assessment: Was the Cold War ever truly 'cold'?
sources.title: Source D (Space Race Propaganda): Astronaut Buzz Aldrin beside the American Flag on the Lunar Surface (20 July 1969)
sources.caption: Astronaut Buzz Aldrin photographed by Neil Armstrong during the Apollo 11 moonwalk on 20 July 1969, standing beside the American flag and the Lunar Module Eagle.
sources.context: The Space Race began with Soviet triumphs: Sputnik (1957) and Yuri Gagarin (1961). President Kennedy committed America to landing a man on the moon before the decade was out. When Apollo 11 touched down, it was hailed as proof that American democracy and free-market capitalism were technologically superior to Soviet communism. **Hinge Question:** Was the Space Race a peaceful scientific adventure, or a thinly disguised competition to prove which superpower had the best rocket technology to deliver nuclear bombs?
sources.provenance: Photographed on color film with a modified 70mm Hasselblad camera on the lunar surface on 20 July 1969; broadcast live to 650 million viewers worldwide.
sources.hinge_question: Was the Space Race a peaceful scientific adventure, or a thinly disguised competition to prove which superpower had the best rocket technology to deliver nuclear bombs?
discussion_ideas: It proved overwhelming American technological, industrial, and economic superiority over the Soviet Union before a global television audience of over 600 million people.

sources.unitTitle: The Cold War & Global Flashpoints (1945–1991)
sources.lessonTitle: Assessment: Was the Cold War ever truly 'cold'?
sources.title: Source E (Historiographical Verdict & Global Map): The Global Cold War and the Proxy Conflicts of the Third World
sources.caption: Cartographic overview of superpower global alignment and proxy battlegrounds across Latin America, Africa, and Asia by 1980, illustrating Professor Odd Arne Westad's argument that the Cold War was a violent global conflict rather than a peaceful European stalemate.
sources.context: Westad’s groundbreaking work forced historians to rethink the traditional narrative. He argued that the true battlefield of the Cold War was not Europe, but the Global South, where the superpowers treated developing nations as disposable chessboard pawns. **Hinge Question:** If over 20 million people died in proxy wars between 1945 and 1991, why do many Western textbooks still describe the Cold War as an era of 'peace'?
sources.provenance: Written by internationally renowned Norwegian historian Odd Arne Westad; published by Cambridge University Press after extensive research in newly opened Russian, American, and Chinese archives.
sources.hinge_question: If over 20 million people died in proxy wars between 1945 and 1991, why do many Western textbooks still describe the Cold War as an era of 'peace'?
discussion_ideas: Historians emphasize that while European capitals avoided nuclear destruction, superpower proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Angola, and Afghanistan claimed over twenty million lives across developing nations.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.1: Supernatural & Religious Explanations of Disease (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source C (Astrological Chart): The Zodiac Man (Homo Signorum), Almanac of Gutun Owain (c.1488–1489)
sources.caption: Illuminated Zodiac Man (Homo Signorum) from the medical and astrological manuscript compiled by Gutun Owain (National Library of Wales, NLW MS 3026C, c.1488–1489), with Middle Welsh labels linking each constellation—such as Aries the ram on the head and Pisces the fish at the feet—to the bodily region it governed.
sources.context: Compiled in Wales around 1488–1489 by Gutun Owain (NLW MS 3026C), this Zodiac Man maps celestial signs directly onto human anatomy using Middle Welsh labels. Medieval physicians argued that God acted as the First Cause who set the planets in motion to influence earthly humours. **Hinge Question:** Why did medieval university physicians combine Christian theology with astrological charts like Source C without seeing any contradiction?
sources.provenance: Compiled by Welsh scribe Gutun Owain at Basingwerk Abbey, c.1488–1489 (National Library of Wales, Aberystwyth, NLW MS 3026C).
sources.hinge_question: Why did medieval university physicians combine Christian theology with astrological charts like Source C without seeing any contradiction?
discussion_ideas: Source C illustrates the medieval belief that every part of the human body was governed by a specific zodiac constellation, from the ram at the head to the two fish tethered to the feet. Physicians consulted such almanac charts to avoid cutting or bleeding a body part while the moon stood in its ruling sign, fearing fatal astrological haemorrhage.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.1: Supernatural & Religious Explanations of Disease (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source D (Material Artefact): Openwork Pewter Pilgrim Badge of St Thomas Becket’s Shrine, Canterbury (c.1350–1400)
sources.caption: Cast openwork pewter pilgrim souvenir badge (c.1350–1400) depicting the gabled, jewel-studded feretory shrine of St Thomas Becket resting atop vaulted arches at Canterbury Cathedral, with an attendant pointing to the reliquary chest.
sources.context: Thousands of cast pewter shrine badges were sold outside Canterbury Cathedral to pilgrims seeking cures at the tomb of St Thomas Becket. Touching the badge to the shrine created a "contact relic" believed to carry the martyr’s miraculous healing grace. **Hinge Question:** Why would a sick medieval peasant spend weeks walking to Canterbury for a pewter shrine badge like Source D rather than paying a local physician?
sources.provenance: Cast lead-tin pewter pilgrim badge sold at Canterbury Cathedral, late 14th century (recovered from the River Thames foreshore, London).
sources.hinge_question: Why would a sick medieval peasant spend weeks walking to Canterbury for a pewter shrine badge like Source D rather than paying a local physician?
discussion_ideas: Source D shows an openwork pewter badge depicting St Thomas Becket’s jewelled reliquary shrine at Canterbury Cathedral, which sick pilgrims bought and pressed directly against the saint’s tomb. Medieval Christians believed this physical contact transferred miraculous healing power into the badge, allowing them to wear it home or touch it against afflicted limbs to seek saintly intercession.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.2: Rational Explanations: Hippocrates, Galen & The Four Humours (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source A (Illuminated Manuscript): Humoral Plant Qualities in the Tacuinum Sanitatis (late 14th century)
sources.caption: Illuminated folio from the medieval health handbook Tacuinum Sanitatis (Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS Nouvelle acquisition latine 1673 / MS Lat. 9333, c.1390), classifying medicinal plants according to their Galenic humoral qualities of cold, heat, moisture, and dryness.
sources.context: Derived from an eleventh-century Arabic medical treatise by Ibn Butlan, the Latin Tacuinum Sanitatis graded herbs, foods, and seasons by their Galenic humoral degrees so wealthy households could preserve humoral balance. **Hinge Question:** Why did the logical, symmetrical neatness of classifying every symptom and plant into four humours convince medieval doctors that no new medical theories were needed?
sources.provenance: Northern Italian illuminated medical manuscript of the Tacuinum Sanitatis, c.1390 (Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris).
sources.hinge_question: Why did the logical, symmetrical neatness of classifying every symptom and plant into four humours convince medieval doctors that no new medical theories were needed?
discussion_ideas: From Source A, it can be inferred that medieval medicine systematically classified every natural plant and foodstuff by its humoral temperature and moisture (hot, cold, wet, or dry). Physicians used illustrated health manuals like the Tacuinum Sanitatis to prescribe cooling or warming herbs that would restore equilibrium to a patient’s unbalanced bodily humours.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.2: Rational Explanations: Hippocrates, Galen & The Four Humours (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source C (Diagnostic Woodcut): Uroscopy Consultation from Johannes de Ketham’s Fasciculo de medicina (1493/1494)
sources.caption: Uncoloured Venetian woodcut from Johannes de Ketham’s medical compendium Fasciculo de medicina (Venice, 1493/1494), depicting a seated university physician seated at a lectern while patients and messengers bring glass urine flasks (matulae) in wicker carriers for humoral inspection.
sources.context: Published in Venice in 1493–1494, Ketham’s Fasciculo de medicina was the first printed book to contain anatomical and diagnostic illustrations. The glass matula became the universal professional emblem of the university-educated physician. **Hinge Question:** How could a medieval physician diagnose a wealthy patient’s humours from a glass matula flask brought by a servant without ever meeting the patient?
sources.provenance: Printed medical woodcut in Johannes de Ketham, Fasciculo de medicina, Venice, 1493/1494.
sources.hinge_question: How could a medieval physician diagnose a wealthy patient’s humours from a glass matula flask brought by a servant without ever meeting the patient?
discussion_ideas: Source C shows messengers bringing wicker baskets of urine flasks (matulae) to a robed university physician seated beneath medical texts. Uroscopy was central to medieval diagnosis because physicians believed the colour, cloudiness, and sediment of urine revealed exact internal humoral imbalances without requiring messy surgical contact.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.3: Approaches to Prevention & Treatment: Rituals, Bleeding & Purging (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source B (Surgical Woodcut): The Phlebotomy "Vein Man" Chart, Fasciculo de medicina (1493/1494)
sources.caption: Woodcut Phlebotomy Chart ("Vein Man") from the Italian edition of Johannes de Ketham’s Fasciculo de medicina (Venice, 1494), mapping dozens of incision points across the human body—from the forehead vein for migraines to ankle veins for reproductive and liver complaints.
sources.context: Because Galenic medicine taught that fevers arose from an overabundance of hot, wet blood, Vein Man diagrams guided barber-surgeons on precisely where to strike with a metal fleam or apply medicinal leeches. **Hinge Question:** Why did patients often interpret feeling weak, cool, and faint after bloodletting as proof that their fever was being cured?
sources.provenance: Printed surgical phlebotomy guide in Johannes de Ketham, Fasciculo de medicina, Venice, 1494.
sources.hinge_question: Why did patients often interpret feeling weak, cool, and faint after bloodletting as proof that their fever was being cured?
discussion_ideas: Source B maps individual surface veins on the head, arms, torso, and ankles directly to printed instructions specifying which illness each incision relieved. Practitioners used these charts to open the exact vein linked to an afflicted organ, draining excess or corrupt blood to restore humoral balance.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.3: Approaches to Prevention & Treatment: Rituals, Bleeding & Purging (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source C (Surgical Manuscript): Instruments and Operative Diagrams from John of Arderne’s Practica (c.1420)
sources.caption: Illuminated surgical folio from an early fifteenth-century manuscript of English master surgeon John of Arderne’s Practica of Surgery (c.1370; copy c.1420, British Library), illustrating specialized metal probes, clyster syringes, and incisions for draining corrupted matter.
sources.context: John of Arderne (1307–1392), often called the father of English surgery, gained battlefield experience during the Hundred Years’ War before practising in Newark and London. His manuscripts depicted clyster enema pipes, probes, and soothing herbal ointments that avoided harsh corrosive cautery. **Hinge Question:** Why did master surgeons like John of Arderne illustrate every instrument to exact scale in the margins of their manuscripts?
sources.provenance: English medical manuscript of John of Arderne (1307–1392), Practica of Fistula in Ano, c.1420 (British Library, London).
sources.hinge_question: Why did master surgeons like John of Arderne illustrate every instrument to exact scale in the margins of their manuscripts?
discussion_ideas: From Source C, it can be inferred that skilled medieval surgeons like John of Arderne designed specialized metal probes, needles, and clyster syringes to drain abscesses and flush corrupt humours from the body. Although surgical craft developed practical tools through battlefield and urban experience, invasive procedures without anaesthetics or antiseptics remained agonising and dangerous.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.4: Medical Care Providers & Monastic Hospitals: ‘Care Not Cure’ (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source A (Surgical Illumination): Medieval Surgeon Treating a Head Wound, Chirurgia of Roger Frugardi (c.1300)
sources.caption: Illuminated surgical miniature from an Anglo-Norman manuscript of Roger of Salerno’s (Roger Frugardi’s) Chirurgia (c.1300, British Library MS Sloane 1977), depicting a practical surgeon inspecting and dressing a deep cranial wound on a seated patient.
sources.context: Created around 1300 (BL MS Sloane 1977), this illumination illustrates practical wound care taught through craft apprenticeship. Unlike élite physicians who studied theoretical Latin texts, barber-surgeons carried out bloodletting, tooth extraction, lancing boils, and wound suturing. **Hinge Question:** Why did medieval society grant lower social status to practical surgeons who stitched wounds than to university physicians who only inspected urine?
sources.provenance: Anglo-Norman illuminated surgical treatise, Roger Frugardi, Chirurgia, c.1300 (British Library, MS Sloane 1977).
sources.hinge_question: Why did medieval society grant lower social status to practical surgeons who stitched wounds than to university physicians who only inspected urine?
discussion_ideas: From Source A, it can be inferred that medieval surgeons performed direct, hands-on physical treatment—cleaning, stitching, and dressing open wounds—which university-trained physicians generally avoided as manual craft labour. Surgeons learned these practical skills through guild apprenticeships and battlefield trauma rather than Latin university lectures.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.4: Medical Care Providers & Monastic Hospitals: ‘Care Not Cure’ (c1250–c1500)
sources.title: Source C (Architectural Record): Tomb of Prior Rahere, Founder of St Bartholomew’s Hospital (Founded 1123; Etching 1818)
sources.caption: Architectural etching by John Coney (1818) recording the medieval Gothic canopy tomb and recumbent effigy of Prior Rahere (d. 1144), who founded both the Augustinian Priory and St Bartholomew’s Hospital at Smithfield, London, in 1123.
sources.context: Founded in 1123 by courtier-turned-monk Rahere after a fever vision on pilgrimage to Rome, St Bartholomew’s Hospital was staffed by Augustinian canons and sisters whose primary duty was Christian hospitality and prayer ("care not cure"). **Hinge Question:** Why did medieval monastic hospitals refuse to admit patients suffering from contagious pestilence or leprosy?
sources.provenance: Etching by John Coney (1818) for Sir William Dugdale’s Monasticon Anglicanum, recording Rahere’s medieval monument in St Bartholomew-the-Great, Smithfield.
sources.hinge_question: Why did medieval monastic hospitals refuse to admit patients suffering from contagious pestilence or leprosy?
discussion_ideas: Source C shows Prior Rahere buried beneath a grand church canopy with kneeling monks reading Latin scripture beside him, reflecting how St Bartholomew’s Hospital (founded 1123) was inextricably tied to an Augustinian priory. Medieval hospitals prioritised "care not cure"—offering clean beds, food, and daily Mass for the patient’s soul and the founder’s salvation rather than surgical intervention.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.5: Case Study: Dealing with the Black Death (1348–1349)
sources.title: Source B (Clinical Woodcut): Physician Attending a Bedridden Plague Victim, Fasciculo de medicina (1493/1494)
sources.caption: Venetian woodcut from Johannes de Ketham’s Fasciculo de medicina (1493/1494) depicting a physician taking the wrist pulse of a bedridden plague victim while holding an aromatic vinegar sponge to his nose and flanked by attendants carrying blazing fumigation torches to ward off miasma.
sources.context: Published in Ketham’s Fasciculo de medicina (1493/1494), this woodcut captures miasma theory in action at the plague bedside: aromatic smoke and scented sponges were used to drive back "corrupt vapours," while fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis) went completely unnoticed in the bedlinens. **Hinge Question:** Why did burning aromatic torches and holding vinegar sponges fail completely to stop physicians contracting bubonic plague?
sources.provenance: Printed medical woodcut in Johannes de Ketham, Fasciculo de medicina, Venice, 1493/1494.
sources.hinge_question: Why did burning aromatic torches and holding vinegar sponges fail completely to stop physicians contracting bubonic plague?
discussion_ideas: From Source B, it can be inferred that physicians believed plague spread through corrupt, poisonous air (miasma) emanating from the sickroom. To purify the air around the bed, attendants held burning aromatic torches while the physician pressed a scented vinegar sponge or pomander over his nose as he checked the victim’s pulse.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT1.5: Case Study: Dealing with the Black Death (1348–1349)
sources.title: Source D (Historical Miniature): The Flagellants Performing Public Penance at Doornik (1349)
sources.caption: Fourteenth-century manuscript miniature depicting the Brotherhood of Flagellants marching into the Flemish town of Doornik in 1349, whipping themselves with iron-tipped scourges to appease God's anger.
sources.context: Contemporary chronicle miniature of Flagellants in Tournai, 1349. Extreme religious penitents whipped themselves in public squares. **Hinge Question:** Why did the Pope and secular kings eventually ban the Flagellants despite their display of intense religious piety?
sources.provenance: Chronicle of Gilles li Muisis, Abbot of Saint-Martin of Tournai, 1349. Royal Library of Belgium.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Pope and secular kings eventually ban the Flagellants despite their display of intense religious piety?
discussion_ideas: Source D demonstrates the extreme religious hysteria triggered by the Black Death. Bands of Flagellants whipped themselves publicly until they bled, believing that voluntary bodily torment would placate God's anger and lift the pestilence.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT2.1: The New Spirit of Enquiry: Humanism, The Printing Press & The Royal Society (c1500–c1700)
sources.title: Source A: Renaissance Printing House with Movable Metal Type, by Jan van der Straet (Stradanus, c.1580)
sources.caption: Sixteenth-century engraving showing the bustling division of labour inside a printing house: compositors setting metal type, proofreaders checking text, and pressmen operating the heavy wooden screw press.
sources.context: Stradanus engraving of a Renaissance printing workshop, c.1580. Movable metal type transformed intellectual life across Europe. **Hinge Question:** Why did the rapid dissemination of medical books by printing presses sometimes reinforce old Galenic errors as well as spreading new anatomical ideas?
sources.provenance: Jan van der Straet (Stradanus), Nova Reperta (New Discoveries), Plate 4: Impressio Librorum, Antwerp, c.1580. Wellcome Collection.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the rapid dissemination of medical books by printing presses sometimes reinforce old Galenic errors as well as spreading new anatomical ideas?
discussion_ideas: Source A depicts an industrialized workshop with multiple workers simultaneously setting type, proofreading, and printing text. This allowed identical copies of medical books to be produced rapidly and affordably, eliminating handwritten scribal errors and Church censorship.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT2.1: The New Spirit of Enquiry: Humanism, The Printing Press & The Royal Society (c1500–c1700)
sources.title: Source E: Robert Hooke’s Microscopic Study of a Flea, Micrographia (1665)
sources.caption: Fold-out engraving of a common flea magnified several hundred times, displaying armored scales, jointed legs, and hairs, drawn by Robert Hooke using his compound microscope.
sources.context: Engraving from Hooke’s Micrographia, 1665. The microscope allowed humans to view biological structures invisible to the naked eye. **Hinge Question:** Why did the discovery of intricate microscopic structures in 1665 fail to lead to any effective new medical treatments for seventeenth-century diseases?
sources.provenance: Robert Hooke, Micrographia: or Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses, London, 1665. Royal Society Library.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the discovery of intricate microscopic structures in 1665 fail to lead to any effective new medical treatments for seventeenth-century diseases?
discussion_ideas: Source E reveals that the compound microscope uncovered an intricate, invisible anatomical world that humans had never seen before, proving that minute insects had complex physical structures and inspiring scientists to observe nature directly.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT2.2: Thomas Sydenham & The Art of Bedside Observation (1676)
sources.title: Source A: Title Page of Thomas Sydenham’s Observationes Medicae (1676; Geneva Edition, 1683)
sources.caption: Latin title page of Thomas Sydenham’s Observationes Medicae circa Morborum Acutorum Historiam et Curationem (originally published in London in 1676; continental Geneva edition printed by Samuel de Tournes, 1683), demonstrating the European reach of Sydenham’s clinical medicine.
sources.context: Title page of Thomas Sydenham's 'Observationes Medicae' (1676). Sydenham classified diseases into distinct species based on meticulous bedside clinical records rather than philosophical humoral balances. **Hinge Question:** Why did Sydenham’s practical, plain-speaking approach alienate many wealthy London physicians who charged massive fees for complex Latin consultations?
sources.provenance: Title page of Thomas Sydenham, Observationes Medicae, printed by Samuel de Tournes, Geneva, 1683 (first London edition 1676).
sources.hinge_question: Why did Sydenham’s practical, plain-speaking approach alienate many wealthy London physicians who charged massive fees for complex Latin consultations?
discussion_ideas: Source A shows that Sydenham published his detailed clinical case histories in Latin under the title Observationes Medicae ('Medical Observations'), demonstrating that he sought to persuade the wider medical profession to adopt systematic bedside recording of acute disease symptoms rather than relying on ancient Galenic theory.

sources.unitTitle: Paper 1: Medicine Through Time with the Western Front
sources.lessonTitle: KT2.2: Thomas Sydenham & The Art of Bedside Observation (1676)
sources.title: Source E: Jan Steen, The Quack (De Kwakzalver, c.1650–1660)
sources.caption: Oil painting The Quack (c.1650–1660, Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam) by Dutch artist Jan Steen.
